artists.alt: A painting in thick palette knife strokes of a woman seen from behind, with a pale blonde bob and bare shoulders, against a deep blue background.
artists.summary: Thickly layered acrylic portraits of women, built entirely with palette knives and spatulas.
artists.dek: A London painter of women's portraits, made with palette knives and spatulas alone. Her thick, sculptural surfaces carry a story about strength, loss and starting again.

sections.title: Biography
sections.html:
Before she painted, Alexandra Johnson worked as a trader. She has described that world as hard, fast and short on feeling, and has said she is a gentler person now.[ap-muse]

The turn came with the death of her mother, to whom she was very close. In interview she links that loss directly to the determination that drove her into painting, working under the name Zara Muse.[ap-muse]

Her portraits have since been hung in luxury hotels, including sites run by the Fairmont group, and in Kanishka, a restaurant in Mayfair. Limited edition prints followed, to bring the work to a wider audience, and collectors in Dubai have begun to buy it.[lno-muse]

I want to champion and support women.Zara Muse, speaking to Luxury News Online, 2025[lno-muse]

Her gallery adds two details we have not been able to check elsewhere, so we give them as the gallery's account: that she has made art since childhood and spent her summer holidays doing so, and that she is the cousin of a well-known street artist. Reported[grove-zm]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Zara Muse paints only with palette knives and spatulas, never brushes. She has called the choice instinctive, made for the depth and richness it gives the surface.[ap-muse]

The result is paint that stands proud of the canvas. Colour is laid in thick, flat-edged slabs rather than blended, so a cheek or a jawline is built from separate planes of saturated colour. Seen close up the face breaks into ridges; from across a room it comes back together.

Her subjects are women, and she has said she wants the work to celebrate the strength and resilience of the women in her own life, her mother included.[lno-muse] Many of the titles are Spanish: Bella Dama del Sol, Luz Serena, Viento del Sur. The gallery describes the work as exploring nature, emotion and human connection through a rich palette.[grove-port][grove-zm]

How to read one

Start with the lit side of the face, where the slabs are thickest and most separate. Count the planes that make the cheek. Then find the shadow side, where she tends to let the knife drag one colour through another. The join between the two is where the portrait either holds together or does not, and in the strongest works it is left slightly unresolved, so the eye keeps working at it.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Alexandra Johnson trained as a trader in the City of London and went on to work as a fund manager.[lno-muse] She took up painting again in 2020, during lockdown, working only with a palette knife and spatula.[ap-muse]

Her paintings reached auction quickly. In Her Own Light, a work of 2023, sold at Tate Ward Auctions in London for £33,750.[ap-muse] The Shape of Stillness, of 2024, sold at Tate Ward on 11 December 2024.[heni-muse-malala] On 3 April 2025 her portrait of Malala Yousafzai sold at Bonhams in London, in the 20th/21st Century Art Day Sale. HENI News gives the price as £51,200, more than six times the low estimate, and Art Plugged gives both £51,000 and £51,200 including premium.[heni-muse-malala][ap-muse]

Luxury News Online described her in 2025 as a resident artist at Grove Gallery in Fitzrovia, London, and reported a commission with the jeweller Astrea London that sets 14.9 carats of diamonds into her portrait Revolution.[lno-muse] Artiscope, which publishes this site, sells her work through Grove Gallery.

sections.title: In her own words
sections.html:
My art is a homage to the resilience and beauty of women.Zara Muse, Art Plugged, 2025[ap-muse]
I've walked in many shoes, and that personal history gives me a deep well to draw from.Zara Muse, Art Plugged, 2025[ap-muse]
I wanted to paint women, their faces, their profile, from all backgrounds, in all of life phases.Zara Muse, Luxury News Online, 2025[lno-muse]

artists.name: Konn Artiss
artists.alt: A square artwork in collage and paint. A large glossy black disc with the name Konn Artiss in white capital letters sits over torn printed paper and thick strokes of yellow, red, black and pale peach paint.
artists.summary: An unnamed artist, or collective, staging public interventions in Venice, Washington and London that question money, fame and the art market.
artists.dek: Nobody has said publicly who Konn Artiss is. What we can document is the work: short-lived, theatrical interventions that turn the money and celebrity around art into the subject of the art itself.

sections.title: Who is Konn Artiss?
sections.html:
The honest answer is that no one has said. Reports differ even on whether Konn Artiss is one person: The Art Newspaper describes an art collective, while other coverage calls it a single mysterious artist and notes that both theories are in circulation.[tan-frieze][fad-ghost]

Anonymity is part of the work. Interventions appear without warning in public space, are photographed and shared, and are gone within days. That pattern has built a mythology around the name, which is itself a subject the work keeps returning to: who gets famous, and why.[ap-antifrieze]

How we report this artistMuch of what is published about Konn Artiss starts with the project's own statements. Where a claim has not been confirmed by an independent source, we mark it Reported rather than state it as fact.

sections.title: Themes and approach
sections.html:
Three ideas run through the work so far: wealth and who controls public space, the art market's habit of turning names into prices, and the fragility of value itself.

The materials are chosen to make those points physical. Ice melts. A newspaper is read and thrown away. An effigy in a canal drifts out of view. The work is designed not to last, which is a pointed choice for an art world built on preserving and reselling objects.[ap-antifrieze]

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
The first work reported under the name was The Washington Ghost, a satirical newspaper with the front-page headline Male Orders Bride. FAD Magazine reported on 23 June 2025 that about 10,000 copies had appeared in Washington DC, at the White House, the Capitol and the offices of The Washington Post, days before Jeff Bezos's wedding in Venice.[fad-ghost] The same report says related work was hung three times in the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, twice in the President's Room. This is reported, and we have not found independent confirmation.[fad-ghost]

In Venice, GB News reported on 25 June 2025 a run of stunts staged every few hours over several days: a Bezos mannequin on a raft near the Rialto Bridge, mannequins of Bezos and Lauren Sánchez in wedding clothes on a gondola on the Grand Canal, and a scarecrow figure in St Mark's Square covered in fake dollar bills printed with his face.[gb-venice]

In October 2025, during Frieze week in London, five ice blocks of about 40 stone each were set in front of the main entrance of Frieze London. Each held a small effigy of Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons or KAWS, and the piece was titled ANTI-FRIEZE.[ap-antifrieze] The Art Newspaper reported more blocks outside galleries and auction houses that week, including one beside a framed picture taped to the window of Phillips.[tan-frieze]

We have found no gallery exhibitions, collections or prizes for Konn Artiss in the sources we have read. The work so far lives in public space and in press photographs.[fad-ghost][ap-antifrieze]

artists.name: Zen Xander
artists.summary: A name with two published descriptions: an anonymous street artist, in one review, and a small group of painters, illustrators, designers and writers, on its own website. The paintings put animals in human situations.
artists.dek: Zen Xander's pictures are quick jokes: a cheetah on a scooter, a lion in a virtual reality headset eating salad. Who makes them is less clear.
glance: Anonymous; described as a collective on its own site

sections.title: Who is Zen Xander?
sections.html:
Reviewing Society Falling in July 2024, Art Plugged introduced Zen Xander as an anonymous street artist moving from the street into the gallery.[ap-zen] The Zen Xander website says instead that the name belongs to a small group of painters, illustrators, designers and writers. This is reported, and we have not been able to settle which account is fuller.[zen-about]

Society Falling, listed by Artsy as a first solo exhibition, ran at Grove Gallery in Fitzrovia from 26 June to 31 July 2024.[artsy-zen] Grove Gallery, which belongs to the same group as this site, also records the work at a Dorsett hotel in London and at South Place Hotel.[grove-exhibitions]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Animals stand in for people. Art Plugged described VR Vegan, in which a lion in a virtual reality headset eats a bowl of salad, as a jab at the gap between real and virtual life and at the contradictions of modern diets. Another work in the show, Always a Cheetah, puts a cheetah on a scooter.[ap-zen]

How to read one

Ask which habit is being laughed at. Using an animal keeps the joke general, so nobody is singled out and anyone can see themselves.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
FAD Magazine announced on 17 May 2024 that Grove Gallery now represents Zen Xander. It described an anonymous street artist who still carries out graffiti stunts while showing in galleries. This is reported, and the article gives no dates or places for the street work.[fad-zen]

The same month Grove Gallery showed Zen Xander with Banksy at Grove at the Grove. Society Falling opened at Grove Gallery Fitzrovia in June 2024.[grove-exhibitions] The sources differ on when it closed: Artsy lists 26 June to 31 July 2024, while Art Plugged, reviewing it on 4 July, gave 9 August 2024.[artsy-zen][ap-zen] In July 2024 the show continued at Dorsett Hospitality London, and the work hung at the opening of the Hilton & Moss showroom. From September 2024 it was shown at South Place Hotel in London with Frank Canvas and Robi Walters.[grove-exhibitions]

Alongside the paintings, Zen Xander releases limited edition prints in drops of three to five versions. Each version carries a different quote, chosen from audience feedback, while the original paintings carry none.[fad-zen][ap-zen]

artists.name: Banksy
artists.alt: A dark statue seen from below against a grey sky: a man in a suit strides off the edge of a stone plinth while a large flag he holds blows back over his face, with scaffolded buildings behind.
artists.summary: An anonymous artist from Bristol's graffiti scene whose stencilled rats, children and chimpanzees moved from walls to canvas and the auction room.
artists.dek: No one has confirmed who Banksy is. The work is easier to pin down: flat black stencils, one accent colour and a dry joke, made on walls since the 1990s and on canvas since at least 2001.
glance: Spray paint, acrylic and emulsion on walls and canvas; screenprints; found objects

sections.title: Who is Banksy?
sections.html:
Banksy has never publicly confirmed who he is. What is documented is where the work began: as a teenage graffiti writer in Bristol in the 1990s, before a move to London.[jsma-banksy] Phillips' catalogue dates the first works on trains and walls to 1993.[phillips-keepout]

The street work was soon joined by work on canvas. Laugh Now, a canvas of 2001, was acquired from the artist by its owner the year it was painted.[bonhams-laughnow] In 2006 he showed large canvases, among them Angel, in the Los Angeles exhibition Barely Legal.[bonhams-angel]

Authentic works are certified by Pest Control, the artist's own authentication body. Each of the recent auction lots we checked was sold with a Pest Control certificate.[bonhams-laughnow][bonhams-angel][phillips-keepout][heritage-ratheart]

How we report this artistAuction catalogues do not agree on Banksy's year of birth: Bonhams gives both 1974 and 1975. We leave it out until it can be settled. We do not give the locations of street works.

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The method is the stencil: a sheet with shapes cut out of it, held to a surface and sprayed through. The Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art calls Banksy an early mainstream innovator of stencil graffiti, a technique valued for its speed and graphic clarity.[jsma-banksy]

On canvas he often mixes spray paint with acrylic or household emulsion.[bonhams-angel][heritage-ratheart] The look carries over from the wall: flat, hard-edged figures in black and white, often with one accent colour, and few or no words.

Animals stand in for people. Rats and chimpanzees recur, and Bonhams' catalogue for Laugh Now describes the chimpanzee as a surrogate through which human hierarchies are seen.[bonhams-laughnow]

How to read one

Look for the single point of colour first, then the gap around it. In Girl with Balloon the red heart sits apart from the black figure, and the empty space between them carries the picture.[wiki-gwb] In Laugh Now the dark figure sits against a pale green ground, and the white placard is the only break in it.[bonhams-laughnow] Our reading: the joke arrives first, and the point follows a second later.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
One well-reported step from the street into museums came in 2009, in his home city. Banksy Versus Bristol Museum opened that summer with about 100 works, free to visit, and ran until 31 August. It had been kept secret since the previous October.[mg-banksy]

The show mixed paintings and sculpture with full-size set pieces, among them an ice-cream van and a ring of portable toilets laid out like Stonehenge.[mg-banksy] Our reading: it was the same joke he makes on walls, moved indoors.

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html: This is the first show I’ve ever done where taxpayers’ money is being used to hang my pictures up rather than scrape them off.Banksy, in a statement on the Bristol show, 2009[mg-banksy]

artists.name: Yayoi Kusama
artists.alt: Close view of Yayoi Kusama's face, with dark hair, red lipstick and pale pink glasses in a decorative silver frame.
artists.summary: A Japanese artist who covered canvases, objects and whole rooms in repeated nets and dots, from the late 1950s until her death in 2026.
artists.dek: Yayoi Kusama made one mark over and over until it filled the surface. The nets of her New York paintings of around 1960 and the polka dots that followed are the same idea at different scales.
glance: Infinity Nets, polka dots, mirror rooms, soft sculpture

sections.title: Who was Yayoi Kusama?
sections.html:
Kusama was born in Matsumoto in 1929 and studied Japanese-style painting in Kyoto in 1948.[wiki-kusama] She moved to the United States in 1957, settling in New York in 1958, and returned to Japan in 1973.[wiki-kusama]

Her painting No. 3P.B. of 1960 was included in the Whitney Museum's annual exhibition in 1961.[tan-kusama-record][artsy-records-nov26] She first took part in the Venice Biennale in 1966 with Narcissus Garden, and represented Japan there in 1993.[wiki-kusama]

She died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August 2026, aged 97. The Yayoi Kusama Foundation announced her death on 27 August.[tan-kusama-obit]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The Infinity Nets are large canvases covered edge to edge in small looped brushmarks, painted over a darker ground.[wiki-kusama] There is no centre and no edge to the pattern: it simply stops where the canvas stops.

Later she gave the same repeated mark the form of a dot and carried it onto objects, sculptures and rooms. The pumpkin became her best-known object, wrapped in dots like a skin.[heni-kusama-pumpkin] In the mirror rooms, reflections repeat lights or dots without end.[wiki-kusama]

How to read one

Stand close to a Net painting first, then step back. Close up you see single loops of paint; from a distance they merge into a surface that seems to move. Our reading: the effect comes from patience, not from any single mark.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Tate's guide to its Infinity Mirror Rooms show fills in the New York years. Her first mirrored installation, Kusama's Peep Show or Endless Love Show, dates from 1966, and in September 1968 she staged a Mirror Performance in New York.[tate-kusama-guide] In that decade she knew Donald Judd, Andy Warhol, Joseph Cornell and Claes Oldenburg, and some of the net canvases ran to 33 feet long.[tate-kusama-dots]

After her return to Japan she chose in 1977 to live in a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo, and kept painting in a studio from nine in the morning until six.[tate-kusama-dots] She also wrote novels and poems there.[tate-kusama-guide] Two of the rooms shown at Tate Modern from 2021 were Infinity Mirrored Room, Filled with the Brilliance of Life, made for Tate's 2012 retrospective, and Chandelier of Grief.[tate-kusama-guide]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
My wish was to be a painter one day.Yayoi Kusama, in a Tate film, 2012[tate-kusama-dots]
I write novels and poems, and I also paint in the hospital. They are my saviours.Yayoi Kusama, quoted in Tate’s exhibition guide[tate-kusama-guide]
I would stand up to them all with a single polka dot.Yayoi Kusama, quoted in Tate’s exhibition guide[tate-kusama-guide]

artists.name: El Anatsui
artists.alt: A weathered grey stone sculpture of a crouching, rounded figure whose large hands cover its face, set on paving in front of a yellow concrete building.
artists.summary: A Ghanaian sculptor in Nigeria who joins thousands of flattened bottle caps with copper wire into hanging metal sheets.
artists.dek: El Anatsui began with wood and clay. Since the 2000s he has been known for large hangings of aluminium bottle caps and copper wire, which fold differently each time they are installed.
glance: Aluminium bottle caps and copper wire; earlier wood and clay
Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, Venice, 2015; Praemium Imperiale, 2017

sections.title: Who is El Anatsui?
sections.html:
Anatsui was born in Anyako, in Ghana's Volta Region, in 1944, and graduated from the College of Art in Kumasi in 1968.[wiki-anatsui] In 1975 he began teaching at the University of Nigeria in Nsukka, where he was professor of sculpture from 1996 to 2011.[wiki-anatsui]

His earlier work was carved wood, clay and found wooden objects. A 2005 exhibition at Skoto Gallery in New York brought the bottle-cap works to wide notice.[wiki-anatsui] He received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2015, and made the Hyundai Commission for Tate Modern's Turbine Hall in 2023.[wiki-anatsui][artnet-anatsui]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The material is the aluminium cap from a liquor bottle. Each cap is flattened, cut or folded, and joined to its neighbours with copper wire.[sothebys-g6][sothebys-hesitant] Thousands of them make a sheet that is heavy but soft enough to hang in folds.

He does not fix how a work should hang. Artnet quotes him saying that life is always in flux, and the works can be draped differently each time.[artnet-anatsui]

How to read one

Look first at the whole: bands and fields of colour, like woven cloth. Then look at one cap, with its printed label still visible. Our reading: the work holds both scales at once, a large abstract surface and the small history of each bottle.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Anatsui studied at the university in Kumasi from 1965 to 1968, and spent more than four decades teaching sculpture at Nsukka.[tan-anatsui-2023] Before the bottle caps there was driftwood: Akua's Surviving Children of 1996 is made from it.[si-anatsui] The October Gallery in London showed the metal hangings in 2002, and the British Museum took Man's Cloth and Woman's Cloth.[si-anatsui]

Within five years the hangings were in the de Young, the Pompidou and the Met, and at Venice in 2007 he hung Dusasa I and II, with another work on the facade of the Palazzo Fortuny.[si-anatsui] In 2019 Second Wave covered the front of the Haus der Kunst in Munich, in the last show curated there by Okwui Enwezor.[si-anatsui][tan-anatsui-2023] The Turbine Hall commission of 2023, Behind the Red Moon, was staged in three acts: The Red Moon, The World and The Wall.[si-anatsui] His studio in Ghana is about 80 metres long.[si-anatsui]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy.El Anatsui, The Art Newspaper, 2023[tan-anatsui-2023]
I have a hidden aim of waking up the artist in everybody.El Anatsui, The Art Newspaper, 2023[tan-anatsui-2023]
You can think of that piece as either a wall or a wave.El Anatsui on Behind the Red Moon, Studio International, 2023[si-anatsui]

artists.name: Beatriz Milhazes
artists.summary: A Brazilian painter who builds dense, layered pictures of flowers, circles and stripes by transferring paint from plastic sheets.
artists.dek: Beatriz Milhazes does not paint straight onto the canvas. She paints shapes on plastic, lets them dry and presses them on, so the finished surface is flat, layered and slightly worn.
glance: Paint transferred from plastic sheets to canvas
Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres, France, 2007

sections.title: Who is Beatriz Milhazes?
sections.html:
Milhazes was born in Rio de Janeiro in 1960 and works there.[wiki-milhazes] She is associated with the 1980s Generation of Brazilian painters.[wiki-milhazes]

She showed at the Carnegie International in 1995 and in Brazil's pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2003. Her first career survey in the United States was at the Pérez Art Museum Miami in 2015.[wiki-milhazes] Her work is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Guggenheim and Tate Modern, among others.[wiki-milhazes]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
She paints each motif on a sheet of plastic. When it is dry, she presses it face down onto the canvas and peels the plastic away, leaving the paint behind.[wiki-milhazes][phillips-paraty] There are no brushstrokes to see, and small tears and wrinkles stay in the surface.[phillips-paraty]

Phillips' catalogue lists her sources as Baroque architecture, lace, Carnival decoration and the plants of Rio's botanical garden, and links her to the Brazilian modernist idea of absorbing outside influences and making them local.[phillips-paraty]

How to read one

Find the geometry first: the bands, grids and circles. Then see how flowers and arabesques sit over and under them. Our reading: the pleasure is in how much is held in balance.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Milhazes studied journalism first, then painting at the Parque Lage school in Rio under Charles Watson.[si-milhazes] In 1984 she was in the group show Como Vai Você, Geração 80?, a show of young Rio painters of the decade.[si-milhazes] She grew up under Brazil's military dictatorship of 1964 to 1985, and has named Tarsila do Amaral as an influence, along with Matisse, Mondrian and Bridget Riley.[si-milhazes][ocula-milhazes]

She worked out the transfer method in 1989, and her studio sits beside Rio's botanical garden.[ocula-milhazes] From 2003 she also made collages using sweet wrappers, and in 2004 she covered the front of Selfridges in Manchester.[si-milhazes] Peeling one painted layer can take up to ten hours.[si-milhazes] In 2023 Turner Contemporary in Margate showed 25 works in Maresias, her first UK museum show in over 20 years.[si-milhazes]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
I think of myself as an abstract geometric artist.Beatriz Milhazes, Ocula, 2015[ocula-milhazes]
I don’t fear colour.Beatriz Milhazes, Studio International, 2023[si-milhazes]
For me, nature is life, and my work has always been in favour of life.Beatriz Milhazes, Studio International, 2023[si-milhazes]

sections.title: Who was S.H. Raza?
sections.html:
Raza was born in 1922 in Kakkaiya, in what is now Madhya Pradesh. He studied at the Nagpur School of Art and then at the Sir J. J. School of Art in Bombay.[wiki-raza] In 1947 he co-founded the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay.[wiki-raza]

He moved to France in 1950 on a French government scholarship and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. In 1956 he became the first artist from outside France to win the Prix de la Critique.[wiki-raza] He moved back to India late in life; Wikipedia gives both 2010 and 2011. He died in New Delhi in July 2016.[wiki-raza]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The early French paintings are landscapes made of blocks: houses, roofs and hillsides set down in thick paint.[saffronart-otta] By the 1960s the forms loosen into large fields of dark colour.[astaguru-provence]

From 1980 the bindu, a central black dot, becomes the centre of his work.[wiki-raza] Around it he sets circles, triangles and bands of flat colour in near symmetry.[saffronart-bindu]

How to read one

In a Bindu painting, start at the dot and move outwards through the rings and bands. Our reading: the picture is built like a diagram of something growing from a seed.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Raza was the son of a forest ranger, and later called the forests of his childhood his most lasting memory.[christies-raza-10] He went to Bombay in 1943.[christies-raza-10] In Paris he met the gallerist Lara Vincy in 1955, and in 1962 he taught at Berkeley in California.[pompidou-raza][christies-raza-10] He married the French artist Janine Mongillat, and went home to India after her death.[christies-raza-10]

The Pompidou's own writers trace the change in the paintings: Adho Man Naadi Dus Bees (1964) and Punjab (1969) belong to the years of loose colour, and the bindu becomes a system from the 1980s.[pompidou-raza] He set up the Raza Foundation in 2001, and was honoured with the Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan and Padma Vibhushan, and the Légion d'honneur.[tan-raza-pompidou][christies-raza-10] In 2023 the Centre Pompidou gave him his first retrospective in a state museum, with more than 90 works.[tan-raza-pompidou]

The most tenacious memory of my childhood is the fear and fascination of Indian forests.S.H. Raza, 2001, quoted by Christie’s[christies-raza-10]
Rothko’s work opened up lots of interesting associations for me.S.H. Raza, quoted by Christie’s[christies-raza-10]

artists.name: Gerhard Richter
artists.alt: Portrait of Gerhard Richter, an older man with white hair, a short white beard and round dark glasses, in a dark coat, looking at the camera.
artists.summary: A German painter who works in two strands: blurred paintings made from photographs, and abstracts dragged across the canvas with a squeegee.
artists.dek: Gerhard Richter works in two ways at once. Some of his pictures copy photographs and blur them; others are made by dragging layers of paint until chance takes over.
glance: Dresden Academy of Fine Arts; Kunstakademie Düsseldorf
Capitalist Realism, with Sigmar Polke and Konrad Lueg
Golden Lion, Venice Biennale, 1997; Praemium Imperiale for painting, 1997

sections.title: Who is Gerhard Richter?
sections.html:
Richter was born in Dresden in 1932 and studied at the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts from 1951.[wiki-richter] In 1961, two months before the Berlin Wall went up, he left East Germany for the West and continued his studies in Düsseldorf.[wiki-richter]

With Sigmar Polke and Konrad Lueg he took up the label Capitalist Realism. He taught at the Düsseldorf academy from 1971 and moved to Cologne in 1983.[wiki-richter] The Museum of Modern Art in New York held a 40-year retrospective in 2002.[wiki-richter]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The photo paintings begin with a photograph, often black and white, copied onto canvas and then softened with a dry brush while the paint is wet.[wiki-richter] Kerze (Candle) of 1982 is one of these, a candle shown in his blurred, photographic manner.[tan-richter-may]

From the mid-1980s he also made abstracts with a large squeegee, pulling layers of paint across the canvas so that colours tear, scrape and show through.[wiki-richter][thevalue-richter-hk]

How to read one

In a squeegee painting, look for the direction of the pull, then for what shows through the gaps. Our reading: the artist sets the conditions, and the paint decides the details.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
The Met's guide to its 2020 Richter show puts the leap west plainly: he was 29 when he left East Germany in 1961 to study in Düsseldorf.[met-richter] That show, Painting After All, gathered more than 100 works from Table (1962) to House of Cards (2020).[met-richter]

One of its centrepieces was Birkenau (2014). It started from four photographs smuggled out of Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1944, and photographs record the paintings in progress between 15 July and 25 August 2014.[met-richter] Our reading: it shows that his abstracts and his photo paintings were never two separate careers.

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
Helplessness is the great theme in painting, or rather the strongest motivation for and during painting.Gerhard Richter, 2014, quoted by the Met[met-richter]
It’s not unusual for me to start from the figurative and end up with something abstract.Gerhard Richter, 2016, quoted by the Met[met-richter]

artists.summary: Brazilian twin brothers who began as graffiti artists in São Paulo and paint one dream world of thin, yellow-skinned figures.
artists.dek: OSGEMEOS paint the same imagined world on walls, canvases and whole buildings: thin yellow figures in patterned clothes, drawn from Brazilian folk culture and hip-hop.
artists.heroCredit: Photo: André Deak for Arte Fora do Museu, CC BY 2.0
glance: Twin brothers Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo

sections.title: Who are OSGEMEOS?
sections.html: OSGEMEOS means “the twins” in Portuguese. Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo started as graffiti artists in São Paulo and now make murals, paintings, sculpture, installations and video.[artsy-osgemeos] They have shown in New York, London, São Paulo, Hong Kong, Seoul and Berlin.[artsy-osgemeos]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Their figures are long-limbed and yellow-skinned, set in surreal landscapes. Artsy links the imagery to Brazilian folklore, hip-hop and graffiti.[artsy-osgemeos] In the studio they mix street materials with others: one 2010 panel combines acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins.[christies-semmedo] Another work of 2005 includes an audio player and headphones.[phillips-andorinha]

How to read one

Look at the clothes and backgrounds first, which are full of small patterns. Our reading: the figures seem calm and dreamy, as if they belong to a world that runs on its own rules.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo were born in São Paulo in 1974 and grew up in Cambuci, a working-class part of the city.[npr-osg][jux-osg] As children they invented their own world, which they call Tritrez.[npr-osg] The Jordan Schnitzer Museum's guide says the yellow of their figures comes from a colour both twins see in their dreams.[jsma-osg]

Their museum career runs through Tate Modern's street art show in 2008, Los Angeles MOCA's Art in the Streets in 2011 and their first US solo show at ICA Boston in 2012.[jux-osg][jsma-osg] At the 2004 Athens Olympics they painted a giant figure in underwear, 82 feet tall.[npr-osg] Segredos at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo (2020 to 2021) showed more than 1,000 items, including their teenage notebooks.[jux-osg] In 2024 the Hirshhorn in Washington opened Endless Story, their first major US museum survey, also with more than 1,000 works.[npr-osg][jsma-osg]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
We are like one artist.Gustavo Pandolfo, NPR, 2024[npr-osg]
There is a conversation in the air flying there, but only we can listen [to] each other.Otavio Pandolfo, NPR, 2024[npr-osg]

artists.name: Vhils
artists.alt: A large portrait of a man in a cap, made by chipping away the pale plaster of a tall brown city wall to show the darker layers beneath.
artists.summary: A Portuguese artist who makes portraits by cutting, drilling and blasting into walls, posters, doors and metal.
artists.dek: Vhils works the opposite way to a painter. He removes plaster, paper or metal until a face appears, so the image is made from the layers of the city itself.
glance: Byam Shaw School of Art and Central Saint Martins, London
Carving, drilling, etching and blasting surfaces

sections.title: Who is Vhils?
sections.html: Alexandre Farto was born in Lisbon in 1987 and began working on the city's walls as Vhils in the early 2000s, according to his own website.[vhils-about] He trained in London at Byam Shaw School of Art and Central Saint Martins.[vhils-about] His studio was founded in 2010 and he reports work in more than 30 countries.[vhils-about]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
His site describes the method as subtraction: cutting, drilling, etching or blasting through a surface rather than adding to it.[vhils-about] He uses walls, billboards, doors, metal, wood, styrofoam, paper and film.[vhils-about] In the studio, stacks of street posters are carved by hand, so the colours of old adverts become the light and shade of a face.[bonhams-attrition]

How to read one

Stand back to see the face, then step close to see the layers. Our reading: the portraits seem to come out of the building's own history.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Vhils told designboom he started illegal graffiti at 13. At 16 or 17 he began to question it, and tried painting billboards white and carving back into them.[db-vhils] He moved to London to study at about 19, and in 2008 took part in the Cans Festival with Banksy.[euronews-vhils-2024]

The studio is in Barreiro, outside Lisbon, with a team of about 15. Hypebeast reports that he began using explosives around 2012, and names the Dissecção train carriages (2014) and the Camadas billboards (2018) among the series.[hb-vhils] His carved faces have gone up from Shanghai and Paris to Los Angeles and Mexico City, and in Rio he worked with an NGO on houses in a favela that was being demolished.[euronews-vhils-2024]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
I felt that by destroying I was revealing.Vhils, designboom, 2017[db-vhils]
All of the layers in my work were a part of someone’s life before.Vhils, Hypebeast, 2020[hb-vhils]
I try to give dignity to these places that were left behind.Vhils, Hypebeast, 2020[hb-vhils]

artists.name: KAWS
artists.summary: An American artist who began by painting cartoon figures onto bus shelter adverts and built a world around his X-eyed character, COMPANION.
artists.dek: KAWS borrows the language of cartoons and toys: flat colour, hard edges and a character whose eyes are always crossed out. The same figure moves between canvases, giant sculptures and editions.
glance: Illustration, School of Visual Arts, New York

sections.title: Who is KAWS?
sections.html: Brian Donnelly studied illustration at the School of Visual Arts in New York and painted backgrounds for television cartoons.[christies-kaws-guide] He tagged KAWS on buildings in New Jersey and Manhattan, then began adding cartoon figures to bus shelter adverts.[christies-kaws-guide] His first toy, COMPANION, followed a trip to Japan in 1999.[christies-kaws-guide]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
His figures are cartoon-like, with crossed-out eyes. Christie's notes comparisons with Basquiat and Haring, who also came from the street, and with Warhol and Koons.[christies-kaws-guide] The paintings crop the figures tight and break them into flat areas of colour.[christies-camo]

How to read one

Look for the X's first, then for the borrowed cartoon. Our reading: a friendly character becomes a little sad or uneasy.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Among the early street works were adverts he altered by painting over them: Untitled (Maidenform) of 1999 is one.[tan-kaws-2021] In 2006 he made a COMPANION for a shop in Tokyo.[rail-kaws] His first exhibition of sculpture alone was at CAC Málaga in 2014.[rail-kaws]

The figures then grew very large. HOLIDAY in 2019 was an inflatable about 121 feet long, floating in Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour, and in 2021 a HOLIDAY hot air balloon of about 140 feet flew in Bristol.[rail-kaws] The same year the Brooklyn Museum gave him his first New York museum show, WHAT PARTY, from February to September.[rail-kaws] Alongside the museum work he has made products with Nike, Uniqlo and Dior, and designed MTV's video music award.[tan-kaws-2021]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
I want you to look at the form. I don’t want you to think about what they might say.KAWS, The Brooklyn Rail, 2021[rail-kaws]
I think no matter what I put on canvas, people don’t think of me as a painter.KAWS, The Brooklyn Rail, 2021[rail-kaws]

artists.summary: An Indonesian artist whose masked, comic-book figures move from walls into paintings, embroidery and batik.
artists.dek: Eko Nugroho draws masked hybrid figures in a bold comic style and makes them in paint, thread and batik, often working with communities around Yogyakarta.

sections.title: Who is Eko Nugroho?
sections.html: Nugroho was born in Yogyakarta in 1977 and lives and works there.[sam-illusion] He often works with communities and other artists to draw attention to social issues.[sam-illusion] He took part in the 5th Asia Pacific Triennial in Brisbane in 2006 and in shows at the Singapore Art Museum and National Gallery Singapore.[sam-illusion]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
His figures come from comic culture and are usually masked. The Singapore Art Museum says the masks are deliberate: he avoids stereotyped faces that could lead to discrimination.[sam-illusion] The same graphic style appears in embroidery and in batik on cotton.[phillips-topi]

How to read one

Read the words in the picture as part of the image. Our reading: the humour carries a serious point about power and society.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Nugroho studied at the Indonesian Institute of the Arts in Yogyakarta and graduated in 2006.[jp-eko][danysz-eko] He was 20 when Suharto fell in 1998, and his first solo show, Bercerobong, was at Cemeti Art House in 2002.[danysz-eko][jp-eko] In June 2000 he started the comic zine Daging Tumbuh.[aa-eko] He has also taught in a primary school, and runs his own art class.[jp-eko]

From 2000 to 2015 he had 14 exhibitions and eight residencies abroad. Among the shows were the Lyon Biennale in 2009 and the Musée d'Art Moderne in Paris in 2012.[jp-eko][danysz-eko][aa-eko] He showed in Indonesia's pavilion at the 2013 Venice Biennale, and the same year Louis Vuitton made 500 scarves from his designs.[aa-eko][jp-eko] His studio employs about 30 people.[jp-eko]

I don’t want to pass judgment on somebody. Such cases can happen to anybody in the future.Eko Nugroho on his masked figures, The Jakarta Post, 2017[jp-eko]

sections.title: Who is Faith XLVII?
sections.html: She began as a graffiti writer called Faith47 on South African streets in 1997. From 2006 she travelled to paint public murals and has made them in 39 countries.[strauss-faith] She has shown at the Calais Museum of Fine Art, the Bernard Magrez Foundation and the Brooklyn Museum.[strauss-faith]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Her work now spans new media installations, hand-sewn wall hangings, bronzes, paintings and prints.[strauss-faith] Wall images return as prints: the lithograph CAPAX INFINITI refers to her 2014 mural on the Carlyle building in Portland, Oregon.[strauss-capax]

How to read one

Read the text first, then the figure. Our reading: the old phrases give everyday subjects a feeling of ritual.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Faith XLVII was born in Cape Town, and her first wall was at the old Clovelly train station, painted with the writer Wealz130.[dm-faith] By the late 1990s and early 2000s she was one of the most active names in South African graffiti.[dm-faith] Two books cover the work: Faith 47 (2011) and Ex Animo (2019), which runs from 2012 to late 2018.[dm-faith]

Animals recur on her walls: a zebra in central Johannesburg, horses on a Los Angeles facade, swans on a Brooklyn roof.[dm-faith] In 2019 she painted The Silent Watcher for Philadelphia's Mural Arts programme.[dm-faith] By 2020 she had been based in Los Angeles for three years, and her solo show CHANT at Everard Read in Cape Town was postponed by lockdown.[dm-faith]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
These are not works made to be pretty or decorative; these are works made to consider, to dismantle, to question.Faith XLVII, Daily Maverick, 2020[dm-faith]
How can one explain in words a language that is not verbal?Faith XLVII, Brooklyn Street Art, 2018[bsa-faith]
One can’t stop the clouds from moving. Nothing is permanent.Faith XLVII, Brooklyn Street Art, 2018[bsa-faith]

artists.name: Vincent van Gogh
artists.summary: A Dutch painter of bold colour and fast, visible brushwork, who made most of his paintings in the last two years of his short life.
artists.dek: Vincent van Gogh painted for little more than ten years and sold little while he lived. In November 2026 one of his last paintings became the most expensive he has ever made at auction.
glance: About 2,100 works, around 860 of them oil paintings

sections.title: Who was Vincent van Gogh?
sections.html:
Van Gogh was born in Zundert in the south of the Netherlands in 1853. In just over a decade of painting he made about 2,100 works, most of them in the last two years of his life.[wiki-vangogh] He had little success while he lived.[wiki-vangogh]

On 16 May 1890 he left the asylum at Saint-Rémy and travelled to Auvers-sur-Oise, north of Paris, wanting to study peasants and landscapes from life.[kmm-chestnuts] He made about 70 oil paintings there in roughly as many days, and died in the village on 29 July 1890 from a gunshot wound he had inflicted himself.[wiki-vangogh] The Van Gogh Museum gave those final months their first full exhibition in 2023.[vgm-auvers-2023]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
His painting is known for bold colour and dramatic, impulsive brushwork.[wiki-vangogh] The Kröller-Müller Museum's description of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, painted in Auvers on 22 and 23 May 1890, shows how deliberate those marks were: flat strokes for the green of the tree, short straight strokes of dark blue to give the leaves structure, thick blue outlines round some of the white blossom, and a sky built from overlapping zigzags. Part of the lower canvas is left bare.[kmm-chestnuts]

How to read one

Our reading: look at one area at a time and ask what kind of stroke it is made of. Sky, foliage and road are often painted in different directions and rhythms, so the brushwork describes the thing as much as the colour does.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
His letters to his brother Theo are the best guide to the last weeks. Around 10 July 1890 he wrote from Auvers about new canvases of wide fields under troubled skies.[letter-649] On 23 July, six days before he died, he sent a sketch of Daubigny's garden and called it one of his most carefully thought-out paintings.[letter-651]

Our reading: the letters do not match the legend of a painter working blind. He describes what he wants a picture to say, and how he set about it.

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
They are vast stretches of corn under troubled skies, and I did not have to go out of my way very much in order to try to express sadness and extreme loneliness.Vincent van Gogh to Theo and Jo, about 10 July 1890[letter-649]
I’m fairly sure that these canvases will tell you what I cannot say in words, that is, how healthy and invigorating I find the countryside.Vincent van Gogh, the same letter[letter-649]
Perhaps you will take a look at this sketch of Daubigny’s garden - it is one of my most carefully thought-out canvases.Vincent van Gogh to Theo, 23 July 1890[letter-651]

artists.name: Wassily Kandinsky
artists.place: Moscow, Munich, Weimar, Dessau and Paris
artists.summary: A Russian-born painter who moved from landscape to pure abstraction, and who believed colour could move a viewer the way music does.
artists.dek: Wassily Kandinsky gave up law for painting at 30 and spent the rest of his life stripping the recognisable out of his pictures. His Bauhaus years produced the hard-edged circles and angles now most closely tied to his name.
glance: Law and economics at the University of Moscow, then painting in Munich
Co-founded the Blue Rider with Franz Marc, 1911; taught at the Bauhaus
Betonte Ecken (1922 to 1923), Christie's New York, 17 November 2026, lot 12 A, US$85,780,000 with fees

sections.title: Who was Wassily Kandinsky?
sections.html:
Kandinsky was born in Moscow in 1866 and studied law and economics at the university there.[bilbao-kandinsky] At 30 he gave up law for art. In 1896 he saw one of Monet's Haystacks and heard Wagner's Lohengrin, and moved to Munich the same year.[agnsw-kandinsky]

In 1911 he founded the Blue Rider with Franz Marc, and in 1912 published On the Spiritual in Art.[agnsw-kandinsky] The First World War sent him back to Moscow in 1914. He returned to Germany in 1921, joined the Bauhaus, and moved to France when the school was closed under Nazi pressure in 1933. He died at Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1944.[bilbao-kandinsky][agnsw-kandinsky]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
From about 1908 he gradually removed recognisable things from his pictures.[agnsw-kandinsky] He wanted painting to be as free of the visible world as music, and wrote about colour as a way of carrying the artist's inner life to the viewer.[agnsw-kandinsky]

Tate describes two main phases: a free, expressive one from 1909 to 1918, and tighter, more geometric compositions from 1921 to 1935.[tate-kandinsky-1958] The second belongs to his Bauhaus years, when lines, circles and angled shapes take over. Betonte Ecken (Accented Corners), made between December 1922 and January 1923, is from the start of that period.[artsy-kandinsky]

How to read one

Our reading: treat the shapes less as objects than as notes. Follow a line from one edge, see where colours press against each other, and notice which forms seem loud and which quiet.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Kandinsky wrote as much as he painted. Besides On the Spiritual in Art there was Point and Line to Plane (1926) and Klänge (1913), with 56 woodcuts.[bilbao-writings] Between 1909 and 1914 he wrote four stage works built on colour and sound, among them The Yellow Sound; none was produced in his lifetime.[bilbao-writings]

In 1928 he staged Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition at Dessau, a production the Guggenheim in New York recreated in 2012.[bilbao-writings]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html: Every work of art is the child of its age and, in many cases, the mother of our emotions.Wassily Kandinsky, opening of On the Spiritual in Art (tr. Michael Sadler)[gutenberg-kandinsky]

sections.title: Who is Rene Matić?
sections.html:
Matić was born in Peterborough in 1997 and graduated in fine art from Central Saint Martins in 2020.[wiki-matic][ual-matic] A show at the South London Gallery followed in 2022.[wiki-matic]

The solo exhibition AS OPPOSED TO THE TRUTH, at CCA Berlin from November 2024 to February 2025, put Matić on the Turner Prize 2025 shortlist.[tate-turner-2025][1854-matic] The prize went to Nnena Kalu.[ma-turner-2025] The same exhibition then won the £30,000 Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize in 2026.[1854-matic] University of the Arts London describes Matić as the second-youngest Turner Prize nominee.[ual-matic]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Tate describes highly personal photographs paired with sound, banners and installation.[tate-turner-2025] The pictures are of the artist's own circle: family, friends and community. A long-running series begun in 2018 carries the title flags for countries that don't exist but bodies that do.[wiki-matic]

How to read one

Our reading: look first at who is in the picture and how close the camera stands. Then look at what hangs around it. The flags and banners turn a private snapshot into something closer to a public statement.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Matić is an artist and writer based in London, working in photography, film and sculpture.[dbpf-matic] The solo shows build up steadily: flags for countries that don't exist but for bodies that do at Arcadia Missa in 2021, soul time at Studio Voltaire and upon this rock at the South London Gallery in 2022, a girl for the living room at the Martin Parr Foundation in 2023, and JAZZ, made with Oscar Murillo, at Kunsthalle Wien in 2024.[dbpf-matic]

The work is held by Tate, the Fondation Louis Vuitton, the Government Art Collection and the Arts Council Collection.[dbpf-matic]

artists.name: Raven Halfmoon
artists.summary: A Caddo Nation sculptor who builds towering double-faced figures in coiled stoneware.
artists.dek: Raven Halfmoon makes stoneware figures by coiling clay by hand, some more than 12 feet tall. Her first touring solo show has travelled to five American venues since 2023.
glance: Ceramics, painting and cultural anthropology, University of Arkansas

sections.title: Who is Raven Halfmoon?
sections.html:
Halfmoon was born in Norman, Oklahoma, in 1991 and works there. She is a citizen of the Caddo Nation and studied ceramics, painting and cultural anthropology at the University of Arkansas.[austin-halfmoon] She spent two years at the Archie Bray Foundation for the Ceramic Arts in Montana.[salon94-halfmoon]

Her first touring solo exhibition, Flags of Our Mothers, opened at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in 2023, then went to the Bemis Center, The Contemporary Austin and the Ogden Museum of Southern Art.[austin-halfmoon][ogden-halfmoon] In 2026 it reached Ballroom Marfa, while she also showed at the Whitney Biennial.[tan-halfmoon]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
She builds her sculptures by coiling clay, from torso size to well over human height, and glazes them.[ogden-halfmoon][salon94-halfmoon] Most are portraits. Flagbearer (2022) is made in three stacked parts and stands more than 12 feet high; The Art Newspaper reports that it took a year to make.[ogden-halfmoon][tan-halfmoon]

How to read one

Our reading: walk all the way round. Many figures have two or more faces, so the work changes as you move, and the marks of the coils stay visible under the glaze.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Halfmoon is a citizen of the Caddo Nation and also has Choctaw, Delaware and Otoe heritage.[tci-halfmoon] At 13 she met the Caddo potter Jeri Redcorn, and later studied anthropology and studio art at the University of Arkansas.[tci-halfmoon]

She told Southwest Contemporary she had gone through about 8,000 pounds of clay by hand, and that a firing can take two to three weeks.[swc-halfmoon] That interview also covers HASINAI (Caddo): Our People (2021) and Weeping Willow Women (2022).[swc-halfmoon] She now works in bronze as well as stoneware. Dancing at Dusk (2024) is travertine, and The Guardians (2024) is a bronze nine feet tall. NEESH + SOKU (MOON + SUN) was her first show with Salon 94.[tci-halfmoon]

sections.title: In their own words

Clay is my most intimate relationship.Raven Halfmoon, Southwest Contemporary, 2023[swc-halfmoon]
I want the process to be seen in the work.Raven Halfmoon, Southwest Contemporary, 2023[swc-halfmoon]
Art is our cultural preservation, it’s how we talk about what’s happening.Raven Halfmoon, The Creative Independent, 2024[tci-halfmoon]

MOCA Los Angeles gave Segovia a solo exhibition from November 2024 to May 2025 and bought one of the paintings.[moca-segovia] Solo shows at C3A in Córdoba and OK Linz followed in 2025, along with a solo booth at Frieze London.[kurimanzutto-segovia][galerie-segovia] In autumn 2026 kurimanzutto in New York showed The Office of Inter-American Affairs Presents, the artist's first solo exhibition there.[eflux-segovia]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
MOCA describes paintings that draw on Mexican cowboy imagery and golden-age cinema to question ideas of masculinity.[moca-segovia] The works are mostly oil on canvas or linen, some of them very wide, and recent projects add digital video and charcoal drawings.[kurimanzutto-segovia]

How to read one

Our reading: find the pose first. Many figures are lifted from films and posters, so ask where you have seen that stance before, then look at what the painting changes about it.

sections.title: Who is Dana Awartani?
sections.html:
Awartani was born in Jeddah in 1987 and lives between Jeddah and New York.[biennale-awartani] She studied at Central Saint Martins and then at the Prince's Foundation School of Traditional Arts in London.[ocula-awartani]

She showed at the 60th Venice Biennale in 2024 and represented Saudi Arabia at the 61st, from 9 May to 22 November 2026, in a pavilion curated by Antonia Carver.[biennale-awartani][eflux-awartani-2026] She has also shown at the Sharjah, Lyon and Diriyah biennials.[artdaily-awartani]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Her work uses painting, sculpture, site-specific installation and performance, and leans on crafts such as geometric drawing, embroidery and dyeing with plants.[ocula-awartani] At Venice in 2024 she showed a large work of silk dyed with herbs and spices, torn and then darned by hand.[biennale-awartani]

How to read one

Our reading: look for the repairs. The stitching, patching and careful geometry take far longer than the damage they answer, and that difference in time is part of what the work is about.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Awartani was born in Jeddah to a Palestinian-Saudi family.[bal-awartani] Her dyed textiles are made with craftspeople in Trivandrum in India, using natural dyes, and she commissions embroidery from Syrian women living as refugees in Jordan.[bal-awartani]

In 2025 she showed in Erasure, a group exhibition that ran until 12 April 2026, with a sand work that grew from Jeddah's old district of Al-Balad. Its title comes from the poet Mahmoud Darwish.[bal-awartani]

sections.title: Who is Jes Fan?
sections.html:
Fan was born in Toronto in 1990, grew up in Hong Kong and studied glass at the Rhode Island School of Design.[biennale-fan][wallpaper-fan] Fan now works between Brooklyn and Hong Kong.[kreps-fan]

The work was shown at the 59th Venice Biennale in 2022 and the Whitney Biennial in 2024. Fan's first New York solo show was at Andrew Kreps Gallery in 2024.[biennale-fan][kreps-fan] Yale University Art Gallery's Jes Fan: Unbounded, from 27 February to 28 June 2026, was the first museum solo exhibition.[yale-fan]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The sculptures join hand-blown glass, resin, fibreglass and 3D prints of body parts with biological substances.[yale-fan][kreps-fan] Form Begets Function (2020), for example, lists urine, depo-testosterone and melanin among its materials.[kreps-fan]

How to read one

Our reading: read the materials list before the title. Much of the meaning sits in what the piece is made of, and the forms often look like specimens or medical models.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
In 2018, on a residency at Recess in New York, Fan worked with melanin made by E. coli bacteria.[wp-fan-2022] The Mother of Pearl series followed from 2020 to 2022, and Fan showed at Socrates Sculpture Park (2019), the Liverpool Biennial and the New Museum Triennial (2021), and in The Milk of Dreams at Venice (2022).[wp-fan-2022]

For the Sigg Prize exhibition at M+ in 2023, Fan showed Sites of Wounding: Chapter 2, a project begun in 2020 around agarwood (Aquilaria sinensis), which also uses 3D scans of the artist's own body.[mplus-fan]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
Art and sciences are essentially just ways of questioning. They are not opposing in my world.Jes Fan, M+, 2023[mplus-fan]
Craft used to be technological; back in the day, the loom was the first computer.Jes Fan, Wallpaper*, 2022[wp-fan-2022]

artists.name: Mohamed L'Ghacham
artists.summary: A muralist from Tangier who paints old family photographs across whole walls.
artists.dek: Mohamed L'Ghacham works from snapshots taken in the late twentieth century, often lent by the people who live where he paints. Since 2017 his walls have appeared at festivals from Mallorca to Vienna.
glance: Graffiti at school, then classical painting

sections.title: Who is Mohamed L'Ghacham?
sections.html:
L'Ghacham was born in Tangier in 1993 and is based in Mataró, near Barcelona.[nuart-lghacham] He came to painting through graffiti at school and then the classical painters.[nww-lghacham] He has named the painters Antonio López and Pere Llobera among his influences.[vaf-lghacham]

He told Colossal that his first murals were painted in abandoned or demolished places, or on the edges of cities.[colossal-lghacham-2021] Since then he has painted for festivals including Saladina Art Fest in Mallorca, North West Walls in Belgium, Vision Art Festival in Switzerland, Nuart Aberdeen and Calle Libre in Vienna.[saus-lghacham][site-lghacham][vaf-lghacham][nuart-lghacham][callelibre-lghacham] He showed with PDP Gallery at the Moniker Art Fair in Brooklyn in 2018.[site-lghacham]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Festival organisers describe figurative painting close to realism, with Impressionist touches, showing everyday scenes taken from late twentieth century photographs.[nuart-lghacham] Colossal noted muted colour, loose layered brushwork, and a liking for photographs with small accidents in them, because they make a scene feel real.[colossal-lghacham-2019] By 2021 he was working from snapshots and home videos lent by neighbours and from city archives.[colossal-lghacham-2021]

How to read one

Our reading: ask whose photograph it was. Many of the walls show the family or the town where they are painted, so the picture belonged to someone who can still walk past it.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
L'Ghacham's parents moved from Tangier to Spain a few months after he was born, and he grew up in Mataró.[jux-lghacham] He started painting in the street in 2008, as factories were closing after the financial crisis, and names Aryz, Gr170 and Kikx among his early influences.[jux-lghacham] Juxtapoz reported in about 2022 that he had recently moved to Madrid.[jux-lghacham]

Colossal lists walls from 2019 and 2020: Confinamiento in Cheste, Matança do porco in Figueiró dos Vinhos in Portugal, Indoor II in Schiedam, Dormitorio III in Mantova, Family portrait in Wevelgem and El dormitorio de Aina in Torrellas.[colossal-lghacham-2021] He has said he would probably have chosen film-making if not painting.[sau-lghacham]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
I almost never depict acted scenes with people posing, I am keen on conveying what is authentic.Mohamed L'Ghacham, Street Art United States, 2017[sau-lghacham]
My paintings usually represent moments of calm and reunion.Mohamed L'Ghacham, Juxtapoz[jux-lghacham]
When I’m on a wall it’s a fight against the clock and you know you have deadlines to meet.Mohamed L'Ghacham, Juxtapoz[jux-lghacham]

artists.summary: The American painter, printmaker and filmmaker who turned supermarket goods, film stars and news photographs into repeated, silkscreened images.
artists.dek: Andy Warhol began as a commercial illustrator. In 1962 he started printing photographs straight onto canvas, and repetition became his subject as much as Marilyn Monroe or a can of soup.

sections.title: Who was Andy Warhol?
sections.html:
Warhol was born Andrew Warhola in Pittsburgh in 1928, the son of Rusyn immigrants from what is now Slovakia. He studied pictorial design at the Carnegie Institute of Technology and moved to New York in 1949, the year he graduated.[wiki-warhol]

His first commercial job was a set of shoe drawings for Glamour. Through the 1950s he drew for magazines such as Vogue and Harper's Bazaar and for the shoe company I. Miller.[wiki-warhol] In 1962 he showed the Campbell's Soup Cans at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles and had his first New York Pop show at the Stable Gallery.[moma-soup][wiki-warhol]

He also made films, managed the Velvet Underground and founded Interview magazine. He survived a shooting in 1968 and died in New York in 1987, after gallbladder surgery.[wiki-warhol]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The Campbell's Soup Cans of 1962 were still painted by hand: 32 canvases, one for each flavour the company sold, with the lettering traced from a projection and the border stamped on.[moma-soup][moma-learning-soup] Later that year he switched to photo-silkscreen, which let him print a photograph onto canvas again and again.[moma-learning-soup][wiki-marilyn-diptych]

That change shows in Marilyn Diptych (1962), made in the weeks after Monroe's death from a publicity still for the film Niagara. The same face is printed 50 times. On the left panel it is bright with colour; on the right it fades to black and white.[wiki-marilyn-diptych]

How to read one

Look at where the print fails: smudges, gaps and colour laid slightly off the photograph. Our reading is that these slips are part of the point. The more often an image is repeated, the less it seems to hold.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Warhol graduated from the Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1949 with a degree in pictorial design and moved to New York to work as a commercial artist. Through the 1950s his illustration clients included Tiffany & Co., The New York Times and Columbia Records, and he won a number of awards for the work.[warhol-life]

In 1962 he made the Campbell's Soup Cans, began his portraits of film stars such as Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley, and started the paintings of car crashes and other disasters known as the death and disaster series. From 1963 he also made films, among them Sleep (1963), Empire (1964), The Chelsea Girls (1966) and the filmed portraits called Screen Tests (1964 to 1966).[warhol-life]

On 3 June 1968 he was shot in the chest at his studio by Valerie Solanas. After he recovered he co-founded Interview magazine. In 1974 he began the Time Capsules, boxes of papers and objects that now number more than 600. Commissioned portraits became a large part of his work in the 1970s and 1980s.[warhol-life]

In the mid-1980s he worked with Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring. The Andy Warhol Museum counts more than 150 canvases made with Basquiat over four years. His Last Supper paintings were shown in Milan early in 1987. He died in New York on 22 February that year, after gallbladder surgery. The museum in Pittsburgh was announced in 1989 and opened in 1994.[warhol-life]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
If you want to know all about Andy Warhol, just look at the surface of my paintings and films and me, and there I am.Andy Warhol, The East Village Other, 1966, as quoted by The Andy Warhol Museum[warhol-life]
Well, I think everybody should like everybody.Andy Warhol to Gene Swenson, 1963, from the full transcript published in the Oxford Art Journal, 2018[sichel-swenson-2018]

Swenson's interview first appeared in ARTnews in November 1963, as part of a series called "What is Pop Art?". Jennifer Sichel's later transcript restores passages that were cut from the printed version.[sichel-swenson-2018]

artists.name: Pablo Picasso
artists.alt: Black and white photograph of the young Pablo Picasso in a heavy overcoat, dark hair over his forehead, looking straight at the camera.
artists.summary: The Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker and ceramicist who, with Georges Braque, broke the picture into flat, angled planes and called it Cubism.
artists.dek: Pablo Picasso worked for almost eighty years. Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, begun in the winter of 1906 to 1907, changed how a body could be drawn, and Guernica, thirty years later, changed what a painting about war could look like.
glance: La Llotja, Barcelona; Royal Academy of San Fernando, Madrid
Paris and the south of France

sections.title: Who was Pablo Picasso?
sections.html:
Picasso's father, José Ruiz Blasco, taught drawing, and he gave his son his first lessons. The family moved to A Coruña in 1891 and to Barcelona in 1895, where Picasso entered the art school known as La Llotja.[brit-picasso]

In 1897 he went to the Royal Academy of San Fernando in Madrid. He found the teaching poor and spent his time in the Prado instead.[brit-picasso]

He first went to Paris in October 1900, with his friend Carles Casagemas. Casagemas's death soon after is linked to the paintings of the so-called Blue Period. By the end of 1901 Picasso had stopped using his father's surname.[brit-picasso] He died at Mougins in 1973, aged 91.[brit-picasso]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
In Les Demoiselles d'Avignon five nude women are built from flat, splintered planes. Their faces draw on Iberian sculpture and African masks, and the two figures on the right are often linked to Picasso's visit to the ethnographic museum at the Trocadéro in Paris while he was working on the picture.[moma-demoiselles]

With Georges Braque he went on to develop Cubism, in which an object is shown from several sides at once and the surface is broken into angled facets.[brit-picasso]

Guernica uses the same language for a public subject. It is painted in greys, black and white, in a long landscape format that the Reina Sofía relates to film and press photography.[reina-guernica]

How to read one

Look for the places where two views of one face meet: an eye seen from the front set into a nose seen from the side. In our reading, that join is where the picture does its work. It asks you to hold two ways of seeing at once.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
After a short spell at art school in Madrid in 1897, Picasso was back in Barcelona by 1899, where he joined the writers and artists who met at the café Els Quatre Gats.[met-picasso-essay] From late 1901 to about the middle of 1904 he painted the pictures now called the Blue Period: poor, lonely figures in a palette that is almost all blue, begun after the suicide of his friend Carles Casagemas.[met-picasso-essay][nga-picasso-early]

He settled in Paris in the spring of 1904, in a run-down building in Montmartre known as the Bateau-Lavoir.[nga-picasso-early][met-picasso-essay] In 1905 he dropped the blues for chalky pinks and reds and turned to circus and fairground performers, the saltimbanques, whom he watched at the Cirque Medrano. This is the Rose Period. The National Gallery of Art names Family of Saltimbanques (1905) as a key work of the period.[nga-picasso-early] Gertrude Stein, whose family supported him, sat for her portrait in 1905 to 1906.[met-picasso-essay]

He painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907 and met Georges Braque the same year. With Braque he worked out Analytic Cubism between 1910 and 1912, then Synthetic Cubism and papier collé, pictures built partly from pasted paper, between 1912 and 1914.[met-picasso-essay]

In the early 1920s he returned to a classical style, and in the late 1920s he took up Surrealist ideas. Guernica was made for the Spanish Pavilion at the Paris exposition of 1937. From the late 1940s he lived in the south of France, where he painted, made prints and ceramics. Retrospectives followed in Tokyo in 1951, in Lyon, Rome, Milan and São Paulo in 1953, and at MoMA in 1957, where the show drew more than 100,000 visitors in its first month.[met-picasso-essay]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
Art is a lie that makes us realize the truth, at least the truth that is given us to understand.Pablo Picasso, "Picasso Speaks", The Arts, New York, May 1923[picassofr-dezayas]
In art, intentions are not sufficient and, as we say in Spanish, love must be proved by facts and not by reasons.Pablo Picasso, "Picasso Speaks", The Arts, New York, May 1923[picassofr-dezayas]

The statement was published unsigned. It is generally attributed to Marius de Zayas, who had helped choose the 83 drawings and watercolours for Picasso's first show in New York, at Alfred Stieglitz's gallery 291 in 1911.[picassofr-dezayas]

artists.name: Jean-Michel Basquiat
artists.alt: Black and white photograph of Jean-Michel Basquiat smiling broadly, in a dark jacket over a pale shirt.
artists.summary: The New York painter who moved from the SAMO© graffiti of the late 1970s to large canvases crowded with words, crowns and fragments of anatomy, all within about eight years.
artists.dek: Jean-Michel Basquiat was 21 when he showed at Documenta in Kassel and 27 when he died. The paintings mix drawing, writing and crossing out, and the words matter as much as the figures.
artists.heroCredit: Photo: Galerie Bruno Bischofberger, 1984, CC BY-SA 4.0

sections.title: Who was Jean-Michel Basquiat?
sections.html:
Basquiat was born in Brooklyn in 1960. His mother was of Puerto Rican descent, and he lived in Puerto Rico from 1974 to 1976. He left school and home at 17.[brit-basquiat]

With Al Diaz and Shannon Dawson he wrote the SAMO© tags that appeared around downtown Manhattan in the late 1970s. His first formal exhibition was The Times Square Show in 1980.[brit-basquiat][whitney-basquiat]

Shows came quickly: Modena in May 1981, Annina Nosei in New York and Larry Gagosian in Los Angeles in 1982, and Documenta 7 in Kassel that summer, where he was among the youngest of 182 artists.[mfa-basquiat-timeline] He met Andy Warhol in 1983, and died of a heroin overdose in his New York loft in 1988.[brit-basquiat]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
By 1980 he was painting on canvas, using oilstick to draw crowns, halos and parts of the body.[whitney-basquiat] He painted on found materials too: LNAPRK (1982) has wooden crossbars, tied with twine, that the Whitney thinks may have come from the street.[whitney-lnaprk]

Words fill the pictures. Many are crossed out, and he explained why.[whitney-hollywood-africans]

I cross out words so you will see them more; the fact that they are obscured makes you want to read them.

How to read one

Read the words before the figures. In Hollywood Africans the lists of crops and film roles carry the argument, and the crown he used as a graffiti writer turns up as a signature.[whitney-hollywood-africans][whitney-lnaprk]

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
SAMO© was listed among the artists in The Times Square Show in June 1980, and Basquiat's work was in New York/New Wave at P.S. 1 early in 1981. His first solo show, titled SAMO, opened at the Galleria d'Arte Emilio Mazzoli in Modena on 23 May 1981.[mfa-basquiat-timeline]

In 1982 he showed at Annina Nosei in SoHo in March, at Larry Gagosian in Los Angeles from 8 April to 8 May, at Documenta 7 in Kassel over the summer, and at the Fun Gallery in the East Village from 4 November.[mfa-basquiat-timeline] The Los Angeles show was his first on the West Coast. That November he moved into Gagosian's house on Market Street in Venice, California.[gagosian-market-street-2024]

Between November 1982 and May 1984 he made about a hundred paintings in Venice, among them Hollywood Africans and Horn Players, and six silkscreen editions with the printer Fred Hoffman. His second Gagosian show, New Paintings, ran from 8 March to 2 April 1983.[gagosian-market-street-2024] He was in the Whitney Biennial that spring, from 15 March to 29 May 1983.[mfa-basquiat-timeline] Gagosian later recalled a wall of seven paintings in that second show, including Hollywood Africans.[tan-basquiat-la-2024]

Mary Boone gave him a solo show in May 1984. His first solo museum show, Paintings 1981 to 1984, opened at the Fruitmarket Gallery in Edinburgh in August 1984 and went on to the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London. A show at the University Art Museum in Berkeley in 1985 was, according to the MFA Boston, the only one a US museum gave him in his lifetime.[mfa-basquiat-timeline]

sections.title: Who was Keith Haring?
sections.html:
Haring grew up in Kutztown, Pennsylvania. His father was an amateur cartoonist. He spent two semesters at the Ivy School of Professional Art in Pittsburgh and had his first solo show at the Pittsburgh Center for the Arts in 1978, aged 19.[pbs-haring]

That year he moved to New York on a scholarship to the School of Visual Arts, and became part of the scene at Club 57 with Kenny Scharf and Jean-Michel Basquiat.[pbs-haring]

He showed at Tony Shafrazi Gallery in 1982 and in the Whitney Biennial in 1983. In 1986 he opened the Pop Shop. He was diagnosed with AIDS in 1988, set up the Keith Haring Foundation in 1989 and died in 1990.[pbs-haring][brit-haring]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The subway drawings were made in white chalk on the black paper that covered unused advertising panels. Britannica calls them unauthorised. PBS counts them in the hundreds over five years.[brit-haring][pbs-haring]

The figures are drawn in one continuous outline, with short lines around them to show movement or noise. The same vocabulary runs through his murals, canvases and prints.[jsma-haring]

How to read one

Count the figures and follow what they are doing to each other. The pictures are simple to see and often not simple to read: in Untitled (Still Alive in '85) figures tumble from a body standing for the year 1985, at the height of the AIDS crisis.[jsma-haring]

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Haring enrolled at the Ivy School of Professional Art in Pittsburgh in 1976 and left after two semesters. In 1978 he had a solo show at the Pittsburgh Arts and Crafts Center, then moved to New York to study at the School of Visual Arts.[haring-fdn-bio]

His first solo show in New York was at the Westbeth Painters Space in 1981. His SoHo debut followed at Tony Shafrazi Gallery in 1982. In the early 1980s he took part in Documenta 7 in Kassel, the São Paulo Biennial and the Whitney Biennial.[haring-fdn-bio]

The Keith Haring Foundation counts more than 50 public works in dozens of cities between 1982 and 1989. They include a mural on the outside of Necker Children's Hospital in Paris, painted in 1987, and one on the western side of the Berlin Wall.[haring-fdn-bio]

The subway drawings are now held by museums. The Museum Brandhorst in Munich has six, one of them still in its original subway frame.[brandhorst-subway] The first major exhibition of his work in the UK opened at Tate Liverpool in June 2019 and travelled to Brussels and Essen.[tateetc-haring]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
Art lives through the imaginations of the people who are seeing it. Without that contact, there is no art.Keith Haring, Flash Art, 1984, quoted in Tate Etc., 2019[tateetc-haring]
They told a story that you could see from a moving train and you could get it.Keith Haring on the subway drawings, interview with John Gruen, 1989, quoted in Tate Etc., 2019[tateetc-haring]

artists.name: David Hockney
artists.alt: David Hockney in a flat cap, round black glasses and a striped cardigan.
artists.summary: The Yorkshire-born painter of California swimming pools, double portraits and, late in life, landscapes drawn on an iPad, who worked in almost every medium he came across.
artists.dek: David Hockney moved between Bradford, London, Los Angeles and Normandy, and between oil, acrylic, photography, photocopiers and tablets. He died in June 2026, aged 88.
artists.heroCredit: Photo: Connaissance des Arts, 2017, CC BY 3.0
glance: Bradford School of Art; Royal College of Art, 1959 to 1962
Companion of Honour 1997; Order of Merit 2012

sections.title: Who was David Hockney?
sections.html:
Hockney grew up in Bradford and studied at the town's art school from 1953 to 1957. He chose the Royal College of Art over the Slade and was there from 1959 to 1962. He showed in Young Contemporaries in 1961.[tan-hockney-obit]

He first went to California in 1963 and spent much of the next forty years there.[tate-bigger-splash] From 2004 he lived in Bridlington and painted the Yorkshire Wolds. During the Covid-19 pandemic he moved to Normandy.[tan-hockney-obit]

He was made a Royal Academician in 1991, a Companion of Honour in 1997 and a member of the Order of Merit in 2012. He died at home on 11 June 2026.[tan-hockney-obit]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
For A Bigger Splash he stapled the canvas to the wall and painted without drawing first. He rolled on the flat areas in two or three layers and used small brushes for the chair, the trees and the splash, which took about two weeks. He worked from someone else's photograph.[tate-bigger-splash]

When you photograph a splash, you're freezing a moment and it becomes something else.

He kept changing tools. In 1987 he made prints on an office colour copier. In 2008 he printed computer drawings by inkjet. In Normandy he drew on an iPad, and the Royal Academy showed 116 of those drawings in 2021.[phillips-hockney-kilham][tan-hockney-obit]

How to read one

Look at how little moves. In A Bigger Splash everything is flat and still except the white burst of water, so the eye goes straight to the one thing that has just happened.[tate-bigger-splash]

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
The Third Love Painting dates from 1960. Art Fund, which supported its purchase for Tate in 1992, links its scrawled surface to the graffiti-like work of Jean Dubuffet. It places the picture at the time Hockney began to take love between men as a subject.[artfund-third-love][dhf-third-love]

In the spring of 2020, during lockdown, he drew the season arriving in Normandy on an iPad. He worked from a house in a field of fruit trees, from the motif and not from photographs, and made at least one drawing a day.[ra-hockney-2021]

The Royal Academy showed the drawings as The Arrival of Spring from 23 May 2021, in an exhibition organised with the Centre for Fine Arts, Brussels.[ra-hockney-2021]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
You have to find out yourself, you have to draw it.David Hockney, RA Magazine, 2020[ra-hockney-2021]
It's ridiculous to think photographs are the ultimate realist picture.David Hockney, RA Magazine, 2020[ra-hockney-2021]
I always wanted to see things as spatial, which photographs never allow.David Hockney, RA Magazine, 2020[ra-hockney-2021]
