artists.name: Damien Hirst
artists.alt: Damien Hirst in a white jacket and red T-shirt, standing in a gallery in front of a wall of large coloured spots.
artists.summary: The British artist known for animals preserved in tanks of formaldehyde, medicine cabinets, and paintings made of spots or spun colour, who won the Turner Prize in 1995.
artists.dek: Damien Hirst's work keeps returning to the same few things: medicine, belief and death. He shows them in glass cases, in rows of pills and in grids of coloured spots.

sections.title: Who is Damien Hirst?
sections.html:
Hirst was born in Bristol in 1965. White Cube counts more than 90 solo exhibitions and over 300 group shows since 1987.[whitecube-hirst]

He won the Turner Prize in 1995. The centre of that show was Mother and Child (Divided), made for the Venice Biennale in 1993.[tate-turner-1995-hirst]

Tate Modern gave him a retrospective in 2012. In 2017 he showed Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable in Venice, a project of almost 190 works that took ten years. Recent museum shows include the Albertina Modern in Vienna in 2025 and the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art in Seoul in 2026.[whitecube-hirst]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
White Cube groups the work into series: the Natural History sculptures of animals in formaldehyde, the medicine cabinets and pharmacy works, the spot and spin paintings, and the butterfly works. It describes his subjects as art, science, religion, love and the knowledge of death.[whitecube-hirst]

The vitrine is his basic unit. The Acquired Inability to Escape (1991) is a glass and steel case holding a chair, a table, an ashtray, a lighter and cigarettes. Nobody is in it, and White Cube reads that absence as the point.[tate-hirst-acquired][whitecube-hirst]

How to read one

Ask what the case or the cabinet is keeping you from. The glass shows you everything and lets you touch nothing. In our reading, that distance does most of the work.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Hirst began a foundation course in Leeds, then took a BA in Fine Art at Goldsmiths in London in the late 1980s. While studying he worked part time at the Anthony d'Offay Gallery.[goldsmiths-hirst]

In 1988, in his second year, he conceived and curated Freeze, a show of his own work and that of fellow Goldsmiths students in an empty London warehouse. Tate dates his first public attention in London to that show.[tate-press-hirst-2012][goldsmiths-hirst]

The spot paintings grew out of collages that his tutor Basil Beattie told him did not belong at art school. Hirst broke them up, and the spots came from that.[goldsmiths-hirst] Gagosian dates the first spot painting, on board, to 1986. In January 2012 it showed more than 300 of them across all eleven of its galleries at once.[gagosian-spots-2012]

In April 2012 Tate Modern opened the first substantial survey of his work in the UK, with more than seventy works.[tate-press-hirst-2012]

sections.title: In their own words

The only place where you didn't have to choose between painting and sculpture.Damien Hirst on why he chose Goldsmiths, interview for Goldsmiths, University of London, undated[goldsmiths-hirst]
Being in art school empowers you to do your own thing.Damien Hirst, interview for Goldsmiths, University of London, undated[goldsmiths-hirst]

artists.name: David Shrigley
artists.alt: David Shrigley in a dark top, looking to one side, in front of a flip chart covered in his line drawings.
artists.summary: The British artist whose deliberately crude drawings, hand-lettered texts, animations and sculptures turn ordinary anxiety into dry jokes. He was shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 2013.
artists.dek: David Shrigley draws badly on purpose. The wobbly line and the crossed-out word are how the jokes land, and the same voice runs through his prints, films and a seven metre bronze thumb.

sections.title: Who is David Shrigley?
sections.html:
Shrigley was born in Macclesfield in 1968 and lives in Brighton.[gla-really-good] He studied at Glasgow School of Art from 1988 to 1991.[artuk-shrigley][tfl-shrigley]

He was shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 2013 for his Hayward Gallery show Brain Activity.[tate-turner-2013-shrigley] He had a solo show at the Pinakothek der Moderne in Munich in 2014, and the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne gave him his first major Australian survey, Life and Life Drawing, from November 2014 to March 2015.[gla-really-good][ngv-shrigley]

In 2016 his bronze Really Good stood on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square.[gla-really-good]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The NGV describes stripped-back, darkly funny drawings that are crude on purpose and deal with dysfunction and anxiety.[ngv-shrigley] The Fourth Plinth programme places the work in the British tradition of satire.[gla-really-good]

Most drawings pair a rough image with hand-lettered words, often with a mistake crossed out and left in. He also makes animations, books, photographs, sculpture and performance.[ngv-shrigley][tate-turner-2013-shrigley]

How to read one

Read the words, then look at the drawing, then read the words again. The joke is usually in the gap between them.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Shrigley was born in Macclesfield in 1968 and grew up in Oadby, near Leicester.[guardian-shrigley-2021] He spent a year at Leicester Polytechnic from 1987, then studied at Glasgow School of Art from 1988 to 1991.[artuk-shrigley][tfl-shrigley] The early work was made in Glasgow: Head Shrinker on Glasgow Green in 1990, a first book, Slug Trails, in 1991, and a show at Transmission Gallery in 1992.[artuk-shrigley]

Solo shows followed in 1997 at The Photographers' Gallery and Stephen Friedman Gallery in London, at Galerie Yvon Lambert in Paris in 1999, at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and Camden Arts Centre in 2002, and at the Kunsthaus Zürich in 2003.[tfl-shrigley] For years his drawings and texts ran weekly in the Guardian's Weekend magazine.[guardian-shrigley-2021]

He lived in Glasgow for 27 years and moved to Brighton in 2015.[guardian-shrigley-2021] He was guest director of the Brighton Festival in 2018.[artsdesk-shrigley-2018] He was made an OBE in 2020.[ngv-really-good-2024] In 2024 the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne bought Really Good through the Felton Bequest, after showing it on the forecourt of NGV International during the NGV Triennial.[ngv-really-good-2024]

Tate's collection page counts 19 works by him, among them Leisure Centre of 1992 and Strive for Excellence of 2013.[tate-coll-shrigley] The British Council Collection lists 12.[bc-shrigley]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
The inquiry continues and it will never end until I'm gone.David Shrigley on drawing, The Guardian, 2021[guardian-shrigley-2021]
The context is half the work.David Shrigley, The Arts Desk, 2018[artsdesk-shrigley-2018]
I am delighted that Really Good has found a permanent home in Australia.David Shrigley, National Gallery of Victoria, 2024[ngv-really-good-2024]

artists.name: Philip Colbert
artists.summary: The Scottish-born painter whose large, crowded canvases are led by a cartoon lobster, his stand-in, and stuffed with emojis, comic-book sound effects and borrowings from pop art and Old Master hunting scenes.
artists.dek: Philip Colbert studied philosophy and ran a clothing label before he painted full time. Then the lobster arrived.
glance: MA Philosophy, University of St Andrews, 2003

sections.title: Who is Philip Colbert?
sections.html:
Colbert was born in Scotland in 1979 and took an MA in philosophy at St Andrews in 2003. He lives in London.[pearllam-colbert-cv] After graduating he set up what he described as an art-inspired clothing brand, and later painted full time.[hypebeast-colbert]

The Saatchi Gallery in London has shown him several times: Hunt Paintings from December 2018 into January 2019, and Lobsteropolis in May and June 2021, which it called his largest UK survey to date.[cw-colbert][saatchi-lobsteropolis] His CV lists group shows at Tate Modern and the Van Gogh Museum in 2015, and a solo show at the Wardlaw Museum in St Andrews in 2021. This is reported by the gallery that published the CV.[pearllam-colbert-cv]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The paintings are large and full. The Saatchi Gallery lists emojis, computer windows, classical architecture, Lichtenstein spots, comic-book sound effects, cactus plants and pixelated mouse cursors among the images.[saatchi-lobsteropolis]

The lobster runs through all of them, crowned and in pyjamas, according to Cent Magazine.[cent-colbert] Colbert puts it simply.

I became an artist when I became a Lobster.

The Hunt Paintings borrow the layout of hunting scenes by Rubens and Van Dyck. In Hunt with Dogs the lobster, holding a devil's pitchfork, rides a unicorn against a man in a tracksuit on a donkey.[cent-colbert]

How to read one

Find the old painting underneath. Once you see the hunting scene or the portrait it is built on, the cartoon details read as comments on it.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Colbert comes from Perth, in Scotland, and studied philosophy at the University of St Andrews. He worked as a fashion designer before turning to painting.[bigissue-colbert-2026]

The Hunt Paintings show at the Saatchi Gallery in London brought together large paintings, sculptures and a virtual reality piece.[hypebeast-colbert] Lobsteropolis was on view at the same gallery until 29 November 2020, during lockdown, and opened with what Hypebeast called the first private view for robots.[hypebeast-lobsteropolis-2020]

In 2026 The Big Issue reported 30 of his sculptures in the Archaeological Park of Pompeii, and a show called The Lost Gardens of Lobsteropolis at The Lightbox in Woking.[bigissue-colbert-2026]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
There's a fascism of seriousness.Philip Colbert, The Big Issue, 2026[bigissue-colbert-2026]
In a Warholian sense, I believe in the power, the poetry of the everyday.Philip Colbert, The Big Issue, 2026[bigissue-colbert-2026]
My paintings, on one hand, are life-affirming and super positive celebrations of hyper-pop language.Philip Colbert on the Hunt Paintings, Hypebeast, 2019[hypebeast-colbert]

artists.name: Los-Talgia
artists.summary: An anonymous collective whose hand-finished objects borrow the colours, plastics and packaging of past decades: game consoles, video sleeves, cassette labels and discontinued snacks.
artists.dek: Los-Talgia does not give names. Grove Gallery, which sells the work, describes a small group of artists from different generations working under one name.

sections.title: Who is Los-Talgia?
sections.html: Almost everything published about Los-Talgia comes from Grove Gallery, which sells the work and belongs to the same group as this site. It describes a collective formed by a small group of artists from different generations, with no names and no hierarchy. This is reported, and we have not been able to check it.[grove-lostalgia]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The gallery says the works act as portals to the objects, colours, textures, packaging and technologies of the eras the members grew up in.[grove-lostalgia]

The Handheld Icon series is the main body of work. Tate Ward's catalogue describes one piece as 3D-printed polymer finished with acrylic and spray paint, resin and applied embellishments, 28 x 23 cm in the artist's frame, with a numbered collector card in an acrylic case. It was one of an edition of 55, each finished differently by hand.[tateward-lostalgia]

How to read one

Look at how the object is presented: graded card, display case, presentation box. In our reading, the packaging is as much the subject as the thing inside it, the way a collectable is kept rather than used.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Grove Gallery, which sells the work, describes Los-Talgia as a collective of artists from different generations, drawing on the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s. It names no members and gives no date or place of founding. This is reported, and we have not been able to check it.[grove-lostalgia]

The known body of work is the Handheld Icon series. Grove Gallery lists pieces numbered from HI-001 to HI-049, each identified by a colour name such as Magenta, Cobalt or Acid, and each shown framed with a certificate card, presentation box and authentication sheet.[grove-lostalgia] The first sale outside the gallery that we have found was at Tate Ward in August 2026, where the catalogue gave the edition as 55 works, each finished differently by hand.[tateward-lostalgia]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
These lines come from the collective's statement on the Grove Gallery page, which sells the work. They are the collective's own account.

los-talgia is not a single artist. it's a collective memory.Los-Talgia, statement on Grove Gallery, read 2026[grove-lostalgia]
we treat nostalgia not as a trend, but as a universal sense of belonging.Los-Talgia, statement on Grove Gallery, read 2026[grove-lostalgia]
we're not recreating the past exactly as it was, we're recreating how it felt.Los-Talgia, statement on Grove Gallery, read 2026[grove-lostalgia]

artists.summary: A London-based artist working under an alias, whose satirical pictures pair a bold image with a one-line title, sold mostly as signed limited edition prints.
artists.dek: Frank Canvas makes pictures that work like captions. Almost everything published about him comes from the gallery that sells the work or from a press release.

sections.title: Who is Frank Canvas?
sections.html:
A press release from Nomad Arts Group, dated 31 December 2022, introduced Frank Canvas as a London-based artist working under an alias and announced his first series, Socially Awkward Elephant, with shows at Quantus Gallery in Spitalfields and in Villars-sur-Ollon in Switzerland. This is reported, and we have not been able to confirm the shows.[prn-frank-canvas]

Grove Gallery records his work at South Place Hotel in London from September 2024, and at the opening of the Hilton & Moss showroom in July 2024.[grove-exhibitions]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
The gallery describes humour, satire and social commentary.[grove-frank-canvas] The titles show it best: Choose Your Reality, Shopaholic, Karma, Coffee, I Like Your Glasses. They point at shopping, caffeine, self-improvement and the phone.[grove-frank-canvas]

The 2022 press release says the first series drew on the design of classic Penguin book covers.[prn-frank-canvas]

How to read one

Read the title first. The image is there to set it up.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Frank Canvas first appeared in public in a press release from Nomad Arts Group dated 31 December 2022. It announced his first series, Socially Awkward Elephant, and said he had shown at Quantus Gallery in Spitalfields, London, and at Grove Gallery in Villars-sur-Ollon, Switzerland. It gave no dates for either show, and it promised a second series for the end of January 2023. All of this is reported by the artist's side, and we have not been able to confirm it independently.[prn-frank-canvas]

The same release describes the original paintings as acrylic on canvas, built up in layers of brushwork and finished with resin.[prn-frank-canvas] The work offered by Grove Gallery today is mostly signed limited edition prints, sold in sizes from A3 to A0.[grove-frank-canvas]

Grove Gallery records his work at the opening of the Hilton & Moss showroom in July 2024 and at South Place Hotel in London from September 2024, alongside Zen Xander and Robi Walters.[grove-exhibitions]

artists.name: Robi Walters
artists.summary: A London artist who cuts petals from broken vinyl records, flyers and packaging and layers them into lotus-like collages, and who has made a painting a day since 2011.
artists.dek: Robi Walters works from what others throw away. Two bodies of work run side by side: slow, exact collages and quick daily paintings.

sections.title: Who is Robi Walters?
sections.html:
Walters was born in London in 1973 and works there. He has spoken publicly about a difficult childhood in care, which The Week and Cent Magazine report, and he told The Week that his art makes little sense without his story.[week-walters][cent-walters]

Cent Magazine reports that the artist Chris Ofili advised him to paint every day, and that since 2011 he has made a painting a day, each named after a news headline. The Hospital Club in London showed them in 2016 as 365: Every Day Counts.[cent-walters] In January 2018 The Week reported that he had opened his own gallery on Ingestre Place in Soho.[week-walters] Grove Gallery gave him a first solo show, A Nation of Millions, in November 2023.[grove-exhibitions]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
He cuts discarded flyers, cardboard, packaging and broken records into petal shapes, hundreds at a time, and layers them outward from a centre. The Week compared the effect to fireworks or a lotus bursting open.[week-walters] Cent Magazine traces the lotus to his first sculpture, a cereal box cut into petals and arranged by sacred geometry.[cent-walters]

How to read one

Stand close. You can still see what the material used to be: a groove from a record, a scrap of lettering, the edge of a label. Then step back and it becomes a flower.

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Walters has no formal art training that we could find. Culture Collective describes him as self-taught.[cc-walters] The daily paintings he began in 2011 grew in places into drawn scrolls, some about 12 by 12 feet, according to The Week.[week-walters] In 2017 Aesthetica described collages built from undelivered flyers for music gigs, magazine and book cuttings, used envelopes and crushed cans, some of them taken from skips. It also reported that he had begun to let others help with production.[aesthetica-walters]

In September 2019 Aston Martin named him its artist in residence for twelve months. The plan was for him to work with material left over from the company's sites at Gaydon, St Athan and Newport Pagnell.[astonmartin-walters] Culture Collective also lists a collaboration with Dr Martens.[cc-walters] A page credited to Walters reports table tops made with the chef Tom Kerridge for his London restaurant at the Corinthia Hotel.[mis-walters]

Sources disagree on where A Nation of Millions was first shown. Grove Gallery lists it as a solo show in Fitzrovia in November 2023.[grove-exhibitions] A page credited to Walters gives Quantus Gallery on Fashion Street, London, from 18 October to 13 November 2023, and describes thousands of hand-cut petals of recycled card and used greeting cards.[mis-walters] In October 2024, during Frieze London, 1 Hotel Mayfair showed a hand-cut installation, Love Supreme, with West Contemporary. This is reported by the hotel group.[onehotels-walters]

sections.title: In their own words
sections.html:
I like the overlaps of colour, or a smudge or a crease.Robi Walters, Aesthetica Magazine, 2017[aesthetica-walters]
I like to use recycled card because it has an energy that something new doesn't have.Robi Walters, The Week, 2018[week-walters]
Time is our most precious resource, and I hope my work serves as a gentle reminder of its value.Robi Walters, 1 Hotels, The Field Guide, 2024[onehotels-walters]

artists.name: Amanza Smith
artists.summary: An American artist, known to television audiences from Selling Sunset, who began painting during a long stay in hospital. Her mixed media canvases mix robotic figures, circuitry and graffiti-like marks.
artists.dek: Amanza Smith came to painting with a public name. The fair test is whether the canvases hold up once you stop thinking about who made them.

sections.title: Who is Amanza Smith?
sections.html:
Smith grew up in Indiana and was a dancer and gymnast before she painted, according to the Majorca Daily Bulletin. The same report says she began painting during a long stay in hospital, when she could use only her right arm.[mdb-amanza]

MASH Gallery in Los Angeles gave her a debut as an exhibiting artist, and lists her other roles, including television and interior design.[mash-amanza] In April 2025 Grove Gallery showed her in London and in Palma, Mallorca.[grove-exhibitions]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Gallery notes for Scattered Remnants and Circuit Riot describe robotic figures, circuitry, glitch effects and graffiti-like marks, with a nod to Basquiat. She calls the robots botsquiats.[mash-amanza] She told the Bulletin that she never starts a canvas with a subject in mind.[mdb-amanza]

How to read one

Look at the layers. Writing, marks and figures sit on top of one another, and some of the writing is her own: Be Happy takes in pages headed On Being Happy.[mash-amanza]

sections.title: Life and career
sections.html:
Smith took up painting at the end of 2023, according to The Tab.[tab-amanza] She also told the Bulletin that an artist who found her on Instagram invited her into a group exhibition of about 14 artists in Los Angeles.[mdb-amanza]

MASH Gallery in West Hollywood describes itself as the place of her debut as an exhibiting artist.[mash-amanza] The Tab reports that one of her paintings was in the gallery's 2024 exhibition Feminine Cadence, and that her work also appeared in its Artful Alchemy and Dazzling Glamor of Creative Pursuit shows.[tab-amanza]

Her first solo exhibition, 404: Humanity not Found, was at Grove Gallery Fitzrovia in London, with 12 paintings according to The Tab. Grove Gallery dates it April 2025 and The Tab says June. The Bulletin, writing on 1 May 2025, placed her London debut in the previous week, which fits April.[grove-exhibitions][tab-amanza][mdb-amanza] Her work was then in Beyond The Surface, the opening exhibition of Grove Gallery Palma in Mallorca, with Zara Muse and Silent Mike, in April 2025.[grove-exhibitions][mdb-amanza]

articles.title: Eleven new portfolios, from Picasso to artists in their first years
articles.dek: World Art Review now covers thirty-four artists. The newest eleven range from the founders of modern art to collectives with a single auction result.
articles.body:
World Art Review now has thirty-four portfolios. The eleven added this month came to us as one list, and it is an odd mix. It runs from Picasso to collectives that have been showing for only a few years.

That range means the portfolios are uneven, and we have not tried to hide it. The older names have museum catalogues, obituaries and decades of auction records behind them. The newer ones have a gallery page, a handful of interviews and sometimes a single sale. Where a fact could not be checked, it sits in the research desk, not in the portfolio.

The long careers

Pablo Picasso, born in Málaga in 1881, built Cubism with Georges Braque.[brit-picasso] Le Baiser, a 1969 painting, sold at Christie's New York in November 2026 for a hammer price of $26.5 million.[tan-christies-20c-2026]

David Hockney died at home on 11 June 2026, aged 88.[tan-hockney-obit] His portfolio follows him from Bradford and the Royal College of Art to Los Angeles, Yorkshire and Normandy.

Damien Hirst won the Turner Prize in 1995.[tate-turner-1995-hirst] David Shrigley, whose drawings look clumsy on purpose, was shortlisted for it in 2013.[tate-turner-2013-shrigley]

From the street to the saleroom

Jean-Michel Basquiat wrote SAMO© graffiti with Al Diaz in the late 1970s, before he was known as a painter.[whitney-basquiat][brit-basquiat] Keith Haring began drawing in chalk on the black paper covering empty advertising panels in the subway in 1981.[brit-haring] Both died young, in 1988 and 1990.

Newer names

Philip Colbert paints crowded scenes led by a cartoon lobster.[saatchi-lobsteropolis] Robi Walters cuts petals from broken records and packaging.[week-walters] Los-Talgia, Frank Canvas, Zen Xander and Amanza Smith have shorter public records, and we say so on each page.[grove-lostalgia][prn-frank-canvas][ap-zen][mash-amanza]

Grove Gallery shows and sells work by several of these artists. Their portfolios follow the same rule as every other: if a fact rests only on the gallery's own word, it is marked as reported.

articles.title: New reviews and artwork explainers for every artist
articles.dek: 20 reviews drawn from published criticism, and 22 close looks at single works. What we added, how we wrote it, and where the gaps are.
articles.body:
Until this month the review section held three pieces and the explainers were mostly about technique. That left most of the artists on this site with a portfolio and nothing else. We have now added 20 reviews and 22 artwork explainers, so that every published artist has at least one longer piece to read.

How the reviews are written

Each review starts from a real exhibition or project and from what named critics wrote about it at the time. Where critics disagreed, we say so and give both sides. Our own view comes at the end and is labelled as ours. Every fact and every quotation links to its source.

How the explainers work

Each explainer takes one work and sets out the basics first: title, date, materials and where it is. Then it points to a few things worth looking at, and only after that says what the work might mean. Where we offer a reading of our own, we say so.

Two gaps

We found no independent published criticism of Zara Muse or Konn Artiss beyond what is already on the site, so each has an explainer but no new review. Artiscope, which publishes this site, sells Zara Muse's work through Grove Gallery, and the explainer says so.

articles.title: Andy Warhol: a portfolio of the artist who made repetition the subject
articles.dek: World Art Review now covers twenty-three artists. The newest died in 1987, and his paintings were the talk of the New York sales this month.
articles.body:
Most portfolios on this site are of living artists. Andy Warhol is the exception, and he earns his place because so much of what came after him, from screenprints to street art, borrows his methods.

He trained in design, drew shoes and fashion for magazines in the 1950s, and then, in 1962, painted 32 soup cans and began printing photographs onto canvas.[wiki-warhol][moma-soup] Marilyn Diptych, from the same year, repeats one publicity photograph 50 times.[wiki-marilyn-diptych]

Why now

Warhol paintings sold in New York four days running this month. At Sotheby's on 16 November a 48 inch Flowers made a reported US$18.2 million with fees.[tan-sothebys-nov-2026] At Christie's on 19 November Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962) made US$9 million with fees.[tan-christies-nov-2026] Our sister site Global Art Monitor lists the details and the gaps.

The portfolio also covers his work with Jean-Michel Basquiat, about 160 paintings made together between 1983 and 1985.[tan-basquiat-warhol]

articles.title: Zara Muse: biography, artistic style and career
articles.dek: From a trading floor to the auction room. How a London painter built a body of sculptural, palette-knife portraits of women, and what to look for in the surface of the work.
articles.credit: Image: Zara Muse portrait, detail. Supplied by Grove Gallery
articles.body:
Some artists arrive through art school, residencies and group shows. Zara Muse arrived from the City. Before she picked up a palette knife, Alexandra Johnson was a trader, in a job she has described as intense and, looking back, soulless.[ap-muse] The paintings she makes now could hardly be further from it: slow, physical, built up by hand, layer on layer.

A change of direction

The change was not planned. Johnson has spoken openly about the death of her mother, to whom she was very close, and about how the grief that followed left her stronger and more determined.[ap-muse] Painting became the place that determination went. She took the name Zara Muse for the work.

That story matters for how we read the paintings. Her subjects are women, and she has said plainly that she wants the work to stand for the strength and resilience she saw in her mother, in herself and in the women around her.[lno-muse]

Knives, not brushes

The most distinctive thing about a Zara Muse painting is how it is made. She works only with palette knives and spatulas, never brushes, a choice she has described as instinctive.[ap-muse] The acrylic goes on thick and is pushed into shape rather than stroked, so each passage of colour keeps a hard edge where the knife lifted away.

Look closely and you see the method. Skin is not blended into soft gradients; it is built from separate, flat planes of strong colour laid side by side. The eye does the blending, which is why the portraits seem to sharpen as you step back from them. The paint has real height, so the way a work is lit changes what you see. A light from the side throws every ridge into shadow.

What to look forStand close, then far. Close up, notice where the knife has dragged one colour through another, and where a fresh, untouched slab sits on top. Far away, notice how few of those slabs it takes to make a convincing face.

From walls to the saleroom

The work found its first wide audience on hospitality walls rather than in museums. Her portraits have hung in luxury hotels, including Fairmont group sites, and in Kanishka in Mayfair, and limited edition prints were introduced so that more people could own one.[lno-muse] The same profile reports the work reaching collectors in Dubai.[lno-muse]

The most widely reported moment came at auction. Her portrait of Malala Yousafzai sold at Bonhams for £51,000. She has said she chose Malala because she sees in her the resilience and courage the work sets out to celebrate.[ap-muse] Her paintings have also passed through the London auction house Tate Ward.[ap-muse]

Reading the career so far

For a collector or a curious reader, a few things are worth holding together. The technique is consistent and recognisable, which is rarer than it sounds. The subject matter is focused. And the career has moved quickly, through commercial interiors and prints as much as through exhibitions. A single strong auction result is a meaningful moment, but it is one data point; the more useful question is how the work develops from here.

Zara Muse is represented by Grove Gallery, which released a new print collection on 4 November 2026.[grove]

articles.title: Konn Artiss: artist profile and selected works
articles.dek: An anonymous name, a sign-off that reads Trust Me, and a run of interventions that put the art market on ice. What we know, what is only reported, and why it matters.
articles.credit: Image: ANTI-FRIEZE, London, 2025. Courtesy Konn Artiss
articles.body:
In the summer of 2025 a name began to appear around stunts aimed at the very rich. By the autumn it had turned up outside the biggest art fair in London. The name was Konn Artiss, and the sign-off attached to it was Trust Me.[fad-ghost]

A name without a face

Nobody has publicly identified who is behind Konn Artiss, and even the basic question of whether it is one person is unsettled. Some coverage describes a single anonymous street artist; The Art Newspaper describes an elusive collective.[fad-ghost][tan-frieze] We use "the artist" in this profile for simplicity, without taking a side.

Selected works

The Washington Ghost, Venice, 2025

Ahead of Jeff Bezos's wedding in Venice, more than 10,000 copies of a satirical newspaper called The Washington Ghost were handed out in the city. Around the same time a mannequin of Bezos was floated through the canals.[gb-venice] The newspaper is the more interesting object: a work that looks like journalism, is given away free, and is meant to be read and thrown away.

The same project ran a staged demonstration in Washington DC. FAD Magazine also reports that work connected to The Washington Ghost was displayed three times at the National Portrait Gallery, including in the room where presidential portraits hang.[fad-ghost] We have not been able to confirm that independently, so we mark it as reported.

ANTI-FRIEZE, London, 2025

During Frieze week, five large blocks of ice appeared outside Frieze London, each holding an effigy of a famous artist: Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS.[ap-antifrieze] Over the following days the ice melted, leaving puddles and debris.

The Art Newspaper also reported blocks of ice placed outside major London galleries and auction houses that week, including a framed image taped to the window at Phillips alongside a block of ice, with the artist comparing the frame to the market's context and the ice to its reality.[tan-frieze]

Reading the workEach piece turns a symbol of permanence into something temporary. Famous names are frozen, like assets kept in storage, and then simply allowed to melt. The work asks what an artist's reputation is worth when nobody is preserving it.

Why it matters

Konn Artiss sits in a long line of artists who use anonymity and public space to criticise the institutions that sell art. What is different is the target: not just the powerful in general, but the art market's own celebrities and prices. Whether the project has staying power, and how it relates to any saleable work, is something we will keep documenting as it develops.

articles.title: Five new portfolios: artists in the early years of their careers
articles.dek: World Art Review now covers twenty-one artists. The five newest are younger than most of the others, and their records are still being written.
articles.body:
Most of the artists on this site have long careers behind them. The five added this month do not. The oldest was born in 1987 and the youngest in 1997. We chose them because each has a body of work that can be described from museum, gallery and prize records, not from popularity online.

Short careers mean thin records. Each portfolio lists what we could not yet confirm in the research desk, and we will fill those gaps as sources appear.

Who they are

Rene Matić photographs family, friends and community in London. The exhibition AS OPPOSED TO THE TRUTH was shortlisted for the Turner Prize 2025 and won the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize in 2026.[tate-turner-2025][1854-matic]

Raven Halfmoon, a citizen of the Caddo Nation, builds stoneware figures by coiling clay. Her touring exhibition Flags of Our Mothers has been to five venues, and Crystal Bridges bought one of her sculptures in 2024.[austin-halfmoon][cb-halfmoon]

Ana Segovia paints figures from Mexican cowboy imagery and cinema. Segovia joined kurimanzutto in 2023 and had a solo exhibition at MOCA Los Angeles in 2024 to 2025.[kurimanzutto-segovia-joins][moca-segovia]

Dana Awartani uses traditional crafts such as darning and natural dyeing. She showed at the Venice Biennale in 2024 and represented Saudi Arabia there in 2026.[biennale-awartani][eflux-awartani-2026]

Jes Fan combines glass and resin with biological materials. Yale University Art Gallery gave the work its first museum survey in 2026.[yale-fan][kreps-fan]

Where to start

For the sculptors, Mixed-media art explains how to read a list of materials. For anyone new to younger artists, How to research an emerging artist shows how we checked these five.

articles.title: Eleven new portfolios, from Bristol to Yogyakarta
articles.dek: World Art Review now covers fourteen artists. Who the new eleven are, what they make, and where to start.
articles.body:
Until this month the review covered three artists, all linked to Grove Gallery in London. It now covers fourteen. The eleven new portfolios follow the same rules as the first three: every fact carries a numbered source, and claims that come only from an artist's own channels are marked as reported.

Six of them started out on walls and streets. The other five made their names in studios and museums. That split is only ours, to make the list easier to read, and some of the artists do not sit neatly on either side.

From the street

Banksy began as a graffiti writer in Bristol in the 1990s and has never publicly confirmed who he is.[jsma-banksy] Authentic works are certified by Pest Control, the artist's own authentication body.[bonhams-angel][phillips-keepout]

OSGEMEOS are the twin brothers Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo, who started as graffiti artists in São Paulo.[artsy-osgemeos] In 2007 they painted the outside walls of Kelburn Castle in Scotland.[hyperallergic-kelburn]

Vhils, the Lisbon artist Alexandre Farto, makes portraits by cutting, drilling and blasting into walls and posters, taking material away rather than adding it.[vhils-about] Much of what is known about him comes from his own website, so his portfolio marks those claims as reported.

KAWS, the New York artist Brian Donnelly, began by painting cartoon figures onto bus shelter adverts. His X-eyed character COMPANION first appeared as a toy after a trip to Japan in 1999.[christies-kaws-guide]

Eko Nugroho was born in Yogyakarta in 1977 and works there. His masked, comic-book figures move from walls into painting, embroidery and batik.[sam-illusion][phillips-topi]

Faith XLVII began as the graffiti writer Faith47 in South Africa in 1997 and has painted public murals in 39 countries since 2006.[strauss-faith]

From the studio

Yayoi Kusama covered canvases, objects and whole rooms in repeated nets and dots.[wiki-kusama] She died in Tokyo on 14 August 2026, aged 97.[tan-kusama-obit]

El Anatsui, born in Ghana in 1944 and based in Nsukka, Nigeria, since 1975, joins flattened aluminium bottle caps with copper wire into large hanging sheets.[wiki-anatsui][sothebys-g6]

Beatriz Milhazes paints each motif on a sheet of plastic, presses it onto the canvas and peels the plastic away, so her pictures show no brushstrokes.[wiki-milhazes][phillips-paraty]

S.H. Raza co-founded the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay in 1947 and spent most of his working life in France. From 1980 his paintings centre on the bindu, a single black dot. He died in New Delhi in 2016.[wiki-raza]

Gerhard Richter works in two strands: blurred paintings copied from photographs, and abstracts made by dragging paint across the canvas with a squeegee.[wiki-richter]

What each portfolio holds

Every portfolio is laid out the same way: a short biography, how the work is made, a few documented works, a timeline and the sources. Each one also says how complete it is, so you can see what we are still checking. What is missing varies. Auction catalogues do not agree on Banksy's year of birth, for example, and several of the international portfolios still rely on encyclopaedia entries for biography while museum pages are found.

Some portfolios mention auction sales. We include them as events in the artist's career, naming the lot and saying whether the price includes the auction house's fees. They are not there to tell you what a work is worth, and we never set a print or an edition against a one-off work.

Where to start

If temporary public work is new to you, read What is an art intervention? before the street portfolios. For the painters, How to look at a painting in ten minutes works with any of them. For El Anatsui and Eko Nugroho, try Mixed-media art.

articles.title: How a Vhils wall portrait is made
articles.dek: Vhils makes faces by taking material away: plaster, paint, posters, wood. A plain guide to the method behind Scratching the Surface.
articles.credit: Image: Joe Hatchiban, carved by Vhils in Berlin, 2011. Photo: OTFW, Berlin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
articles.body:
Artist: Vhils (Alexandre Farto). Series: Scratching the Surface, from 2007, first shown publicly in Lisbon that year and at the Cans Festival in London in 2008.[vhils-about]

The idea

Most portraits are made by adding paint. Vhils removes material. He has called himself "kind of an urban archaeologist", carving into the walls of the city instead of painting on them.[euronews-vhils-2024] He began as a teenager by painting over billboards and cutting back through the layers of posters, and found that "by destroying I was revealing".[db-vhils]

How it is done

The face is cut into the surface, chipping away paint and plaster to reach the layers beneath, so the picture is drawn in depth and in the different colours of the wall's past. Tools range from chisels and power tools to explosives, which he began to develop around 2012.[hb-vhils][euronews-vhils-2024] His studio in Barreiro, outside Lisbon, has a team of about fifteen.[hb-vhils]

The same method works on other surfaces. Doors of Cairo, shown beside the Pyramids in 2025, used 65 salvaged doors.[colossal-vhils-cairo]

What to look at

The layers. Each depth of cut shows a different colour from the wall's past: paint, plaster, brick.

Distance. Up close the face is rubble and scars. Across the street it resolves into a likeness.

Who it is. The faces are usually people from the place, not celebrities. Vhils has said a single face can stand for a community.[colossal-vhils-cairo]

What it means

Vhils has said that every layer he cuts through "was a part of someone's life before".[hb-vhils] Our reading: the portraits are about the city as much as the sitter. The building gives up its history to make a face.
articles.alt: A large portrait of a man in a cap, made by chipping away the pale plaster of a tall brown city wall to show the darker layers beneath.

articles.title: The Silent Watcher, explained
articles.dek: A nineteen-storey woman looks down over West Philadelphia. How Faith XLVII's largest mural was made, where it is, and what is written on it.
articles.credit: Image: a different mural by Faith XLVII, Cologne, photographed 2015. Photo: Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
articles.body:
Artist: Faith XLVII, with Beth Clevenstine. Date: 2019. Where: 3901 Market Street, Philadelphia, on University Square, an affordable housing block for older people. Size: 11,000 square feet, nineteen storeys high. Commissioned by: Mural Arts Philadelphia.[muralarts-silent]

What it shows

A woman looks down at the street "with a caring gaze", in Mural Arts' words.[muralarts-silent] Geometric lines, a colour gradient and touches of gold lead the eye upwards. The mural carries the words "Philadelphia Maneto", from the city's seal, which means "Let Brotherly Love Endure". Lights keep it visible after dark.[muralarts-silent] It was her first mural in Philadelphia.[streetsdept-silent]

What to look at

The face. The local blog Streets Dept praised how she carries small details of face and body up to a huge scale: "Her work is brilliantly painterly."[streetsdept-silent]

The gold. It marks the lines that pull the eye up the building, away from the street.

The words. A civic motto, painted on housing for older people, at the gateway to a university district.

What it means

Mural Arts says the artist drew on the neighbourhood's cultural, historical and social life.[muralarts-silent] Our reading: the title does the work. A watcher who is silent is neither a guard nor a camera. She offers attention without control, which fits Faith XLVII's own description of her work as made "to consider, to dismantle, to question".[dm-faith]
articles.alt: A tall painted figure in a dark hooded robe, face lifted and lit from one side, fills the pale green end wall of a block of flats. Bare trees stand in front and ivy climbs the brick beside it.

articles.title: Love Is in the Bin, explained
articles.dek: A painting that half destroyed itself the moment it sold, then sold again for eighteen times as much. What happened, and what you are looking at.
articles.body:
Artist: Banksy. What it is: a framed canvas of Girl with Balloon, partly shredded by a device hidden in its frame in 2018. Sold again: Sotheby's London, 14 October 2021.[tan-litb]

What happened

Girl with Balloon began as a stencil on a wall near Waterloo Bridge, in 2002.[wiki-gwb] A framed canvas version came up at Sotheby's in October 2018. Seconds after the hammer fell at about £1 million, a shredder hidden in the frame pulled the canvas down and cut the lower half into strips.[tan-litb][npr-banksy] The work was renamed Love Is in the Bin. Sotheby's said it had no warning.[npr-banksy]

In 2021 the buyer sent the shredded work back to auction. It made £16 million on the hammer, or £18.6 million with fees, a record for the artist at the time.[tan-litb]

What to look at

The two halves. The top is untouched: a girl in black and white reaching for a red heart-shaped balloon. The bottom hangs below the frame in thin vertical strips.

The colour. The balloon is the only red in the picture. It stays whole, in the upper half, while the girl's lower body is cut away.

The frame. It is an ornate gilt frame. It held the shredder, so the frame is as much part of the work as the canvas.

What it means

This is our reading. The prank was aimed at the auction room, where a picture becomes a price. It failed on its own terms: destroying the work made it famous and more expensive. That failure is now the subject of the piece. You are looking at a joke about the art market that the art market absorbed.

Glasgow's 2023 show Cut & Run included a detailed model of how the shredder worked.[tan-goma-2023]

articles.title: Infinity Mirrored Room, Filled with the Brilliance of Life, explained
articles.dek: A dark room, a shallow pool, mirrors and hundreds of small lights. How Kusama's best-known mirror room works, and where it came from.
articles.body:
Artist: Yayoi Kusama. Date: 2011/2017. Materials: mirrored walls, a shallow pool of water and hundreds of coloured LED lights. Collection: Tate, presented by the artist, Ota Fine Arts and Victoria Miro in 2015.[tate-kusama-guide][tateetc-kusama]

How it works

You walk along a narrow path over a shallow pool. The walls are mirrors. Small lights hang from the ceiling at different heights. Each light is reflected in the walls and the water, then reflected again, so a room a few metres across seems to run on without end.[tate-kusama-guide] The lights change colour and pulse. Tate's guide compares them to "a heartbeat or a ticking clock".[tate-kusama-guide]

What to look at

Your own reflection. You appear in the work many times over, and quickly lose track of which reflection is nearest.

The water. It doubles the room downwards as well as sideways, so there is no floor to anchor you.

The rhythm. Stay still and watch one light. The changes are slow, and the room feels different at the end of a visit than at the start.

Where it came from

Tate traces the mirror rooms back to Phalli's Field of 1965, and before that to the Infinity Net paintings, in which one looping brushmark is repeated across a whole canvas.[tateetc-kusama] Kusama said of those years: "I painted nets from dawn to dusk."[tateetc-kusama] The room was made for her Tate retrospective in 2012.[tate-kusama-guide]

What it means

Our reading: the room is a painting you stand inside. The net paintings asked the eye to lose its place in a field of marks. The mirror room does the same to the whole body. Whether that feels calm or unsettling depends on the visitor, and critics have reported both.[ribaj-kusama][week-kusama]

articles.title: Old Man's Cloth, explained
articles.dek: From a distance it looks like woven gold. Close up it is thousands of flattened bottle tops held with copper wire. How El Anatsui's metal cloths are made.
articles.body:
Artist: El Anatsui. Date: 2003. Medium: aluminium and copper wire. Size: 487.7 by 520.7 cm. Collection: Harn Museum of Art, Gainesville, Florida.[smarthistory-oldmans]

How it is made

The metal comes from the tops and neck labels of liquor bottles, collected near the artist's home in southern Nigeria. Each piece is flattened, cut or folded and joined to the next with copper wire, usually corner to corner.[smarthistory-oldmans] Anatsui first used bottle tops instead of wood in Man's Cloth and Woman's Cloth of 2001.[artfund-anatsui] By 2023, in Tate's Turbine Hall, as many as 200 people were working on a single hanging.[tate-anatsui-guide]

The work is laid flat while it is made. When it is installed it is pushed, folded and draped, so it never hangs the same way twice.[smarthistory-oldmans]

What to look at

From across the room. Bands of gold, red and black suggest a woven cloth. Smarthistory compares it to a large woven hanging.[smarthistory-oldmans]

Close up. Brand names and printed colours survive on the flattened metal. Every square was once a bottle.

The edges. They are uneven and jagged, not hemmed. Smarthistory singles this out as unusual.[smarthistory-oldmans]

What it means

Smarthistory links the bottle tops to the long and painful history of trade between Africa and Europe, including the Atlantic slave trade.[smarthistory-oldmans] Art Fund describes Anatsui's use of cloth as a metaphor for both the fragility and the strength of tradition.[artfund-anatsui] Our reading: the work is easy to love for its shimmer, and the bottle tops are there to remind you what the shimmer cost.

articles.title: Maresias, explained
articles.dek: Beatriz Milhazes' large 2002 painting gave its name to her UK survey. Here is how its flat, layered circles were made, using a method she invented.
articles.body:
Artist: Beatriz Milhazes. Date: 2002. Medium: acrylic on canvas. Size: 300 by 267 cm. Collection: TBA21, Thyssen-Bornemisza Art Contemporary.[artsdesk-milhazes] It was one of the large paintings in Brazil's pavilion at the 2003 Venice Biennale.[tate-milhazes-2024] Tate glosses the title as the salty sea breeze.[tate-milhazes-2024]

How it is made

Milhazes calls her method monotransfer. Around 1989, frustrated by visible brushstrokes, she began painting her motifs onto sheets of plastic, then pressing them paint side down onto the canvas and peeling the plastic away.[tate-milhazes-2024][artlyst-milhazes] The result is a perfectly flat skin of colour. Because each motif is made separately, the layers build up one over another and the surface can crack.[artsdesk-milhazes]

What to look at

The circles. Targets, discs and rings of dots overlap edge to edge. One critic wrote that "each circle spirals and spins into another".[artsdesk-milhazes]

The surface. Look for faint cracks and peeled edges. No brushstroke is visible anywhere, which is the point of the method.

Distance. Walk towards it slowly. The picture changes from a single pattern to separate layers as you get closer.[churchtimes-milhazes]

What it means

Critics have read the circles as rosary beads, lace and carnival decoration, drawing on Rio's churches and carnival.[churchtimes-milhazes][artsdesk-milhazes] Milhazes calls herself an abstract geometric artist.[ocula-milhazes] Our reading: both are true. The forms are geometric, and the memories come in through colour.

articles.title: Raza's bindu, explained
articles.dek: For the last thirty years of his career S.H. Raza painted a black circle at the centre of the canvas again and again. Where it came from, and how to read one.
articles.body:
Artist: S.H. Raza. Example: Bindu, 2002, acrylic on canvas, 40 by 40 cm.[saffronart-bindu] The bindu became a systematic part of his painting from the 1980s.[pompidou-raza]

The road to the dot

Raza arrived in France in 1950.[pompidou-raza] For years he painted landscape: French villages such as Village Otta Corse of 1958, then large dark canvases such as La Provence Noire of 1965.[saffronart-otta][astaguru-provence] Saurashtra of 1983, a canvas 200 cm square named after the peninsula in Gujarat, was described at its sale in 2010 as a bridge into the geometric work that followed.[deshgujarat-saurashtra] It sold at Christie's London for £2,393,250 and went to Kiran Nadar.[deshgujarat-saurashtra]

What to look at

The centre. A solid black circle sits in the middle of the canvas, often the darkest and flattest thing in it.

What surrounds it. Bands, triangles and squares of colour are arranged around the dot, often symmetrically, so the eye keeps returning to it.

The edges. In many late works the paint is kept clean and the forms hard-edged, a long way from the village landscapes of the 1950s.

What it means

Raza linked the bindu to Indian thought about origin and energy, and once said of it, "It's the centre of my life."[christies-raza-10] He is reported to have said that he learned how to paint from France, and what to paint from India.[tan-raza-pompidou] When the Centre Pompidou showed his work in 2023, one review warned against turning his personal beliefs into general claims about Indian thought.[aap-raza] Our reading: take the black dot first as a painter's device. It is a fixed point that lets him try endless arrangements of colour around it, the way a musician might hold one note.

articles.title: Birkenau, explained
articles.dek: Four large abstract paintings from 2014 hide four photographs taken inside a death camp. What Richter did, and why you cannot see the pictures beneath.
articles.body:
Artist: Gerhard Richter. Date: 2014. Medium: oil on canvas, four paintings. Size: 260 by 200 cm each. Collection: on loan from the Gerhard Richter Kunststiftung to the Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin.[flashart-richter]

The source

In 1944 four photographs were taken secretly at Auschwitz-Birkenau and smuggled out of the camp.[met-richter] Studio International describes them as the only four surviving photographs taken by inmates. Richter first tried to copy them onto canvas, and was not satisfied.[si-richter-2025]

How it was made

The Met published photographs of the work in progress, dated through the summer of 2014. They show Richter sketching the photographs onto the canvases, then gradually covering them with layers of paint, white and black, then green, red, pink and coral, spread and scraped across the surface with wide squeegees.[met-richter] By the end, the photographs are buried.

What to look at

The colours. Mostly grey and black, with red and green breaking through. Joe Lloyd, in Studio International, reads the grey as smoke, the red as blood and the green as nature.[si-richter-2025] That is his reading, and Richter has not confirmed any code.

The scraping. Look for places where one layer has been dragged off to show another. The Met calls them "heavily disturbed, ruptured surfaces".[met-richter]

What is missing. There is no figure, no camp, no recognisable shape at all.

What it means

Our reading: the paintings are about refusing to make the photographs into a painting. Richter is best known for blurred paintings made from photographs, such as Uncle Rudi of 1965.[tan-richter-flv] Here the subject was too grave to blur, so he covered it. The four canvases record that he started, and that he chose to stop. They are abstract paintings with a known subject that can no longer be seen.

articles.title: 1980, explained
articles.dek: Three teenagers on a graffiti-covered New York subway car, painted partly in sequins. How OSGEMEOS turned a memory of the streets into a shimmering panel.
articles.body:
Artists: OSGEMEOS (Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo). Date: 2020. Medium: mixed media with sequins on MDF. Size: 219 by 319 by 5 cm. Shown in Endless Story at the Hirshhorn, 2024 to 2025.[bmore-osg][hirshhorn-osg]

What it shows

Three young men ride a New York subway car covered in tags. One holds a Krylon spray can.[bmore-osg] The title is a year from the twins' childhood: they were born in São Paulo in 1974.[npr-osg]

What to look at

The sequins. They catch light as you move, so a picture of a dirty train flickers like a stage costume.

The support. MDF is a cheap building board, more like a wall than a canvas. It suits painters who started on walls.

The figures. Compare them with the yellow-skinned figures of the murals. The same cast moves between walls, trains and panels.[bmore-osg]

What it means

Our reading: it is a homage and a memory at once. Painting a tagged New York train in sequins turns a rough subject into something treasured, the way a childhood memory is polished by time. The work honours graffiti while admitting it is now a museum subject.

articles.title: COMPANION, explained
articles.dek: A cartoon body, a skull and crossbones for a head and X marks for eyes. How KAWS' best-known figure went from a toy to a bronze, and what critics make of it.
articles.body:
Artist: KAWS (Brian Donnelly). First made: 1999, as a vinyl toy. Example: COMPANION (ORIGINALFAKE), 2011, fibreglass and paint, 245 cm high, edition of three plus two artist's proofs.[christies-companion]

Where it came from

KAWS began by painting over advertisements, as in UNTITLED (MAIDENFORM) of 1999, where a model's head is replaced with a COMPANION head.[tan-kaws-2021] The figure has a body borrowed from Mickey Mouse and a skull for a head.[globe-kaws] A version made for his Tokyo shop, ORIGINALFAKE, followed in 2006.[rail-kaws]

How it has grown

The figure now appears at every scale. COMPANION (RESTING PLACE) of 2013 is split down the middle, cartoon on one side and anatomy on the other.[tan-kaws-2021] A 35 metre inflatable floated in Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour in 2019.[tan-kaws-2021] In FAMILY of 2021, a painted bronze, four of his figures pose as a family.[ago-kaws]

What to look at

The eyes. Two Xs. In cartoons they mean a character is dead or knocked out. Here they make the face unreadable.

The pose. Many recent figures cover their face with their hands or slump. The Globe and Mail's critic saw COMPANION used as an everyman, a parent and a mourner.[globe-kaws]

The surface. Even bronze is painted to look like plastic. Paddy Johnson found this the weakness of the sculptures.[tan-kaws-2021]

What it means

KAWS told the Brooklyn Rail: "I want you to look at the form. I don't want you to think about what they might say."[rail-kaws] Our reading: that is the trouble and the appeal. A figure without a readable face lets anyone project a feeling onto it, which is why it sells, and why critics find it hard to pin down.

articles.title: Illusion, explained
articles.dek: A large embroidery in the Singapore Art Museum, stitched with masked figures and factory chimneys. How Eko Nugroho turned gang-jacket embroidery into a picture of a damaged landscape.
articles.body:
Artist: Eko Nugroho. Date: 2007. Medium: embroidery. Size: 296 by 148 cm. Collection: Singapore Art Museum.[sam-illusion]

How it is made

Nugroho draws the design and the stitching is done with a community of artisans in Indonesia. The National Heritage Board's record says he took the idea from the embroidered patches on Indonesian gang leather jackets.[gac-illusion] He began making embroideries in 2007, the year of this work.[artandmarket-eko]

What it shows

A stripped landscape with machine-like monsters and a masked figure.[sam-illusion] A chimney recurs as a sign of industry and pollution. The record quotes the artist describing "the language of industry, factory, work, pollution and chaos".[gac-illusion]

What to look at

The thread. Dense, glossy stitching, closer to a badge or a uniform patch than to a sampler.

The masks. Nugroho's figures are almost always masked. He has said he does not want to pass judgement on anyone.[jp-eko]

The empty ground. Look at how much of the landscape is bare. The monsters stand in a place that has been used up.

What it means

Our reading: the material carries the argument. Gang patches are badges of belonging, made to be worn on the street. Nugroho turns that craft into a wall-sized picture of what industry leaves behind. A form of street identity becomes a form of protest.

articles.title: Sunflowers, explained
articles.dek: Fifteen flowers in a jug, painted in about a week in August 1888 to decorate a room for a guest. How Van Gogh made a picture almost entirely in yellow.
articles.body:
Artist: Vincent van Gogh. Date: 1888. Medium: oil on canvas. Size: 92.1 by 73 cm. Collection: The National Gallery, London, bought in 1924.[ng-sunflowers]

Why it was painted

Van Gogh painted it in Arles to decorate his house before Paul Gauguin came to stay. Gauguin arrived on 23 October 1888.[ng-sunflowers] He made seven versions of the subject in 1888 and 1889: four in August 1888, in about a week, and three more in January 1889.[ng-sunflowers]

What to look at

The stages of the flowers. The National Gallery counts fifteen sunflowers, from bud to full bloom to heads gone to seed.[ng-sunflowers] Some are fresh, some are dying. The picture shows a lifetime in one jug.

The yellows. Yellow flowers in a jug on a mustard table against a pale wheat-yellow wall. Van Gogh described it as "a picture all in yellow".[ng-sunflowers] The differences between the yellows are what hold the shapes apart.

The paint. The gallery notes that the stiff new tube paints let him build thick ridges, or impasto. Look at the seed heads, where the paint is piled up.[ng-sunflowers]

The signature. "Vincent" is written in blue on the jug, as if it were part of the decoration.[ng-sunflowers]

What it means

The National Gallery offers three readings: the old Dutch tradition of flower paintings as reminders of death, the flowers as a sign of friendship, and simple delight in the life of nature.[ng-sunflowers] Van Gogh himself wrote, as the gallery quotes him, "The sunflower is mine."[ng-sunflowers] Our reading: the friendship and the dying flowers sit together. It was a welcome for a guest, painted by someone who knew the flowers would not last the month.

In 2024 the painting hung beside the Philadelphia version, with a blue background, for the first time since 1963.[tan-vangogh-2024]

articles.title: Composition 8, explained
articles.dek: Circles, triangles and lines on a pale ground, painted at the Bauhaus in 1923. Kandinsky thought it his best work since the war. How to look at a picture with no subject.
articles.body:
Artist: Wassily Kandinsky. Date: July 1923. Medium: oil on canvas. Size: 140 by 201 cm. Collection: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, Founding Collection.[bilbao-comp8]

Where it sits

Kandinsky painted it while teaching at the Bauhaus. The Guggenheim's guide says he regarded it as "the high point of his postwar achievement".[bilbao-comp8] Solomon Guggenheim bought it at Dessau in 1929, the first of more than 150 Kandinskys the museum came to own.[bilbao-comp8] Studio International notes the influence of Malevich and Rodchenko on this geometric phase.[si-kandinsky-bilbao]

What to look at

The circles. The largest, upper left, is dark with a ring of colour. Smaller circles are scattered across the canvas. The guide notes that they point to the circle paintings that followed.[bilbao-comp8]

The lines. Thin, straight and crossing, some ruled into grids, some ending in points. They work like a drawing laid over the colour.

The triangles. Sharp, often in pairs, pointing up or across. In the guide's words, "circles, triangles, and linear elements create a surface of interacting geometric forms".[bilbao-comp8]

The ground. Pale and fairly even, so every shape reads clearly. Compare Black Lines of 1913, which is dense and crowded.[bilbao-kandinsky]

What it means

The Guggenheim guide opens with a line from Kandinsky's 1911 writing on colour, which compares the effect of colour to a piano: "Color is the keyboard, the eyes are the hammers, the soul is the piano with many strings."[bilbao-comp8] Our reading: there is no hidden subject to find. Look at it the way you would listen to a piece of music, following which shape leads and which answers, and the picture makes sense.

articles.title: Untitled (No Place for Violence), explained
articles.dek: A huge white flag, hung in the middle of Matić's Turner Prize room. What the words say, where they came from, and why a flag was the right form.
articles.body:
Artist: Rene Matić. Date: 2024. Form: a large white flag. Shown: AS OPPOSED TO THE TRUTH, CCA Berlin, and the Turner Prize 2025 exhibition, Cartwright Hall, Bradford.[tan-turner-2025][tateetc-turner-2025]

What it says

One side reads "No Place". The other reads "For Violence". Kadish Morris, writing for Tate Etc., explains that the phrase echoes what Joe Biden and Barack Obama said after the attempt on Donald Trump's life in July 2024.[tateetc-turner-2025]

What to look at

The two sides. You can never read the whole phrase at once. Walk around it and the sentence splits into two claims.

The placing. In Bradford it hung from the ceiling in the centre of the room, so every other work was seen past it.[tateetc-turner-2025]

The sound. Millie Lacey reported audio from pro-Palestinian protests, naming the daily dead in Gaza, playing in the room and cutting across the flag's message.[sota-turner-2025]

What it means

Matić has said the aim was to "embarrass the kind of principle of what a flag is supposed to be".[tan-turner-2025] Morris reads it as a flag that pledges allegiance to no state.[tateetc-turner-2025] Our reading: a flag usually claims ground. This one borrows the words politicians use after violence and makes them literal, a flag for "no place". Put next to recordings of a war, the words start to sound hollow, which is the point.

articles.title: Flagbearer, explained
articles.dek: A stoneware woman more than twelve feet tall, built from coils of clay and fired in three parts. How Raven Halfmoon made her largest work.
articles.body:
Artist: Raven Halfmoon. Date: 2022. Medium: stoneware and glaze, in three stacked parts. Size: 388.6 by 149.9 by 121.9 cm. Made during a residency at California State University, Long Beach.[ogden-halfmoon]

How it is made

Halfmoon builds with thick coils of clay, joined by pressing and scraping with her hands.[sixty-halfmoon] A figure this large will not fit in a kiln whole, so it was built and fired in three pieces and stacked.[sixty-halfmoon] The Brooklyn Rail gives its weight as 2,400 pounds.[rail-halfmoon] Firing can take two to three weeks.[swc-halfmoon]

What to look at

The hand marks. Halfmoon leaves them on purpose. "You can see the moment that I laid down the mark," she says.[rail-halfmoon]

The colour. A red base, a white middle dripping onto the red, and a pale top. The Brooklyn Rail reads red as the soil of Oklahoma and as a reference to murdered Indigenous women.[rail-halfmoon][sixty-halfmoon]

The name. "Halfmoon" is written in black across the work. River Ian Kerstetter reads it as a shift from graffiti's "I was here" to "I am here".[sixty-halfmoon]

What it means

The figure is an Indigenous woman. Halfmoon is a citizen of the Caddo Nation, and the work honours Caddo women and the matrilineal tradition in which she carries her mother's family name.[tci-halfmoon][sixty-halfmoon] At the Bemis Center it stood outside, facing towards Norman, Oklahoma, according to the curator quoted by Kerstetter.[sixty-halfmoon] Our reading: the size is not there to impress. It makes a woman impossible to overlook, in a country where Indigenous women have often been unseen.

articles.title: The Ramón paintings, explained
articles.dek: A cowboy seen from hip to knee, face always hidden, with titles that do not match the picture. How Ana Segovia uses cropping to unpick the macho film hero.
articles.body:
Artist: Ana Segovia. Series: Ramón, 2025, oil paintings. Shown: kurimanzutto's solo booth at Frieze London, October 2025.[nyt-segovia][another-segovia]

Who Ramón is

Ramón is an invented cowboy, described by The New York Times as a Mexican Marlboro Man.[nyt-segovia] Segovia starts from film stills, many from the golden age of Mexican cinema, and from images found online.[galerie-segovia-2025][nyt-segovia]

What to look at

The crop. The pictures show the body from hips to knees. You never see Ramón's face.[nyt-segovia]

The titles. Titles such as Ramón Eating an Apple or Ramón Playing the Flute promise an action you cannot see. Of Ramón Throwing a Rock, the Times notes simply: "There is no rock."[nyt-segovia]

The surfaces. Jeans and chaps are painted in reflective reds, and the Times reads the effect as openly erotic.[nyt-segovia]

What it means

Segovia names three things that drive the work: "humor, eros, and aggression".[another-segovia] And of the character: "Ramón is my fantasy of who I want to be, or think I am."[another-segovia] Our reading: the cropping does two things at once. It takes away the hero's face, his authority. And it puts the viewer in the position of someone looking at a body with desire, a position western films rarely admit to. The joke is affectionate, which is why it lands.

articles.title: Come, let me heal your wounds. Let me mend your broken bones, explained
articles.dek: Torn silk, dyed with herbs and spices, then darned by hand. How Dana Awartani's Venice installation records destroyed buildings, one repair at a time.
articles.body:
Artist: Dana Awartani. Date: 2024. Medium: darning on medicinally dyed silk. Size: 520 by 1250 by 297 cm. First shown: 60th Venice Biennale, Arsenale, 2024.[designboom-awartani][biennale-awartani]

How it is made

Long panels of silk are dyed with herbs and spices chosen for their healing properties, a method linked to the textile traditions of Kerala that Awartani studied.[designboom-awartani] Holes are torn in the silk, each one standing for a historic or cultural site damaged or destroyed by war in Gaza and across the Arab world. Each hole is then darned by hand.[designboom-awartani]

What to look at

The holes. Each is a place. Count them, and remember that the work is added to as new sites are lost. The writer Saira Ansari, quoted by designboom, describes this as making room for newer documentation.[designboom-awartani]

The darning. The mends do not hide the damage. They leave a visible scar in a different texture.

The colour. The silk hangs in long yellow and red lengths, and each repair shows as a change of texture in the colour.[designboom-awartani]

What it means

Darning is a humble household repair. Awartani has said that some people see craft as a form of prayer.[bal-awartani] Our reading: the work sets the slowness of mending against the speed of destruction. It cannot keep up, and it does not pretend to. That honesty is what makes it moving.

articles.title: Palimpsest, explained
articles.dek: Chinese characters implanted in live oysters, grown into pearls, then fired between plates of glass. Jes Fan's five-minute film about healing and what it hides.
articles.body:
Artist: Jes Fan. Date: 2023. Medium: HD film, colour, sound, 5 minutes 39 seconds. Shown: Sites of Wounding: Chapter 1, Empty Gallery, Hong Kong, 2023.[eflux-fan-wounding]

What happens in it

The film follows a research project of nearly three years with scientists at the University of Hong Kong. Four Chinese characters, meaning "Pearl of the Orient", an old nickname for Hong Kong, were implanted in live oysters. The oysters were later fired in a kiln between plates of glass. There are panoramas of Hong Kong harbour and a wordless, close-up soundtrack.[eflux-fan-wounding]

What to look at

The oysters. An oyster makes a pearl by coating something that has got inside it. The pearl is a response to an injury.

The writing. The words are hidden inside the growth. You know they are there, but you cannot read them.

The sound. No narration. The film gives you process, not explanation.

What it means

Wong Binghao, reviewing the show for e-flux, wrote: "Like the pearl it protects, this artwork reveals its meaning only in glimpses."[eflux-fan-wounding] The oyster was the first subject of Fan's long project on how bodies regenerate at sites of injury, which went on to include agarwood.[eflux-fan-wounding][mplus-fan] Our reading: the film is about Hong Kong as much as oysters. A city's name for itself is planted in a living thing, covered over and then put through fire. What survives is beautiful, and the message is sealed inside.

articles.title: Casa Paquita, explained
articles.dek: A forty-year-old family snapshot, painted back onto a wall in the place where it was taken. How Mohamed L'Ghacham turns other people's photographs into murals.
articles.body:
Artist: Mohamed L'Ghacham. Date: 2017. Where: Can Picafort, Mallorca. Made for: Saladina Art Fest.[saus-lghacham][colossal-lghacham-2019]

The source

The mural was painted from a photograph of the owner's children taken about forty years earlier, in the same spot.[saus-lghacham] Colossal describes his habit of working from old family photographs and choosing the accidental shots, for their honesty.[colossal-lghacham-2019]

What to look at

The faces. They are suggested with loose, layered strokes rather than drawn in detail. Colossal notes that you need to step back for them to come together.[colossal-lghacham-2019]

The colour. A muted palette, close to a faded print, which ties the picture to its weathered wall.[colossal-lghacham-2019]

The place. The scene is back where it happened. Anyone who knew the family sees the past and present at once.

What it means

L'Ghacham has said that his paintings "usually represent moments of calm and reunion".[jux-lghacham] Our reading: this is a mural that only fully works for a few people, and that is its strength. Strangers see a warm, ordinary scene. The family sees itself forty years younger, painted larger than life on the wall of home.

articles.title: Marilyn Diptych, explained
articles.dek: Fifty copies of one publicity photograph, in colour on the left and fading black and white on the right. Made in the months after Marilyn Monroe died.
articles.body:
Artist: Andy Warhol. Date: 1962. Medium: silkscreen ink and acrylic paint on canvas. Size: 205.4 by 289.6 cm. Collection: Tate, bought in 1980.[wiki-marilyn-diptych]

How it was made

Warhol began making silkscreens in August 1962, the same month Monroe died.[tate-warhol-conservation] The source was a publicity still for the film Niagara (1953), taken by Gene Kornman. Warhol cropped it to her face, had it made into a screen, painted some areas by hand and then printed the face over the colour.[tate-warhol-conservation] Wikipedia quotes his description of the screen process: the photograph is transferred in glue onto silk, and you "roll ink across it so the ink goes through the silk but not through the glue".[wiki-marilyn-diptych]

It was first two separate pieces. Tate says the collectors Burton and Emily Tremaine bought them, and Phaidon reports that it was Emily Tremaine who put them together and asked Warhol if it could be a diptych.[tate-warhol-conservation][phaidon-marilyn]

What to look at

The left panel. Twenty-five faces in yellow hair, lavender skin and orange ground. The colour is laid on in blocks and does not quite line up with the printed face.[phaidon-marilyn]

The right panel. Twenty-five black and white faces. Some are heavy with ink, others so faint they nearly vanish.

The grid. Fifty repeats of one image, like a contact sheet or a shop shelf.[wiki-marilyn-diptych]

What it means

A diptych is a two-panel painting, a form long used for religious images. Phaidon links the title to that tradition and to the way Monroe was worshipped.[phaidon-marilyn] Our reading: the two halves look like fame and death, the bright public image on one side and the fading prints on the other. Warhol said he wanted "more of an assembly line effect".[phaidon-marilyn] The fading is what happens when an assembly line runs out of ink, and here it reads as grief.

After two years of conservation Tate now shows it looking "closer to how Warhol and the Tremaines would have seen it in 1962".[tate-warhol-conservation]

articles.title: The Venice canal effigy, explained
articles.dek: In June 2025 a floating figure of Jeff Bezos drifted through Venice ahead of his wedding. How the Konn Artiss stunt was staged, and what it was for.
articles.body:
Artist: Konn Artiss. Date: June 2025. Form: a mannequin of Jeff Bezos on a raft in the canals of Venice, with a satirical newspaper, The Washington Ghost.[gb-venice]

What happened

GB News reported a figure of the Amazon founder floating on a raft near the Rialto Bridge, apparently steered by a hidden propeller. The appearances were repeated every three hours over several days. Earlier, mannequins of Bezos and Lauren Sánchez in wedding clothes had floated along the Grand Canal in a gondola, and another Bezos figure appeared in St Mark's Square as a scarecrow covered in fake dollar bills bearing his face.[gb-venice] GB News also reported more than 10,000 copies of The Washington Ghost, with the headline "Male Orders Bride".[gb-venice]

What to look at

The movement. A figure that drifts, appears and vanishes on a schedule behaves more like a performance than a sculpture.

The setting. The figures turned up at the best-known sights, the Rialto, the Grand Canal and St Mark's Square, where they were sure to be seen and photographed.

The paper. The title plays on The Washington Post, and the headline turns the wedding into a joke about mail order.

What it means

Our reading: the target is not only one rich man but the way a city can be hired as a backdrop. The work lasted only as long as the wedding. Like ANTI-FRIEZE, it was made to be photographed and shared, then to disappear. As with all Konn Artiss work, much of what is known comes from press reports, and the artist's identity has not been confirmed.[tan-frieze]

articles.title: Zara Muse's portrait of Malala Yousafzai, explained
articles.dek: A portrait built from palette-knife slabs of acrylic, and the painting that took Zara Muse into a Bonhams sale. What we know, and what we do not.
articles.body:
Artist: Zara Muse. Subject: Malala Yousafzai. Medium: acrylic on canvas. Sold: Bonhams London, 20th/21st Century Art Day Sale. The interview that reports the sale gives £51,200 including the buyer's premium in one place and £51,000 in another.[ap-muse] We have not found the date or size of the painting in a source we could check.

How it is made

Muse paints with palette knives and spatulas only, never brushes.[ap-muse] The paint is laid in thick, flat-edged slabs rather than blended, so the face is built from separate planes of colour. Our guide to palette-knife painting explains the technique in more detail.

What to look at

The planes of the face. Look at how the cheek and jaw are made from distinct strokes of colour, each with a hard edge left by the knife.

The ridges. Seen from the side, the paint stands proud of the canvas.

Distance. Close up the face breaks into slabs. From across a room it comes together.

Why this subject

Muse has said: "I chose Malala Yousafzai because, to me, she is such a powerful subject." She describes her work as "a homage to the resilience and beauty of women".[ap-muse]

What we cannot say

We have found no independent review of the painting. The account above comes from an interview with the artist and from Grove Gallery, which represents her. Artiscope, which publishes this site, sells her work through Grove Gallery.[ap-muse] We have marked it accordingly, and we would welcome a catalogue entry or lot page to confirm the details.

articles.title: Understanding palette-knife painting
articles.dek: What a knife does that a brush cannot, how painters use it, and how to read the ridges it leaves behind.
articles.body:
A palette knife was first a mixing tool: a thin, flexible blade for blending colours on the palette before they went anywhere near the canvas. At some point painters noticed that the knife could also put paint on, and that it left marks no brush could make.

Knife or brush: what changes

A brush holds paint in its bristles and releases it gradually, leaving fine grooves and soft, feathered edges. A knife carries paint on a flat steel surface and lays it down all at once. That gives three effects that define the technique:

  • Clean, hard edges. Where the blade lifts, the paint stops. Colours sit side by side rather than melting into each other.
