  • Height. A knife can lay paint thickly and leave it standing. This thick paint is called impasto.
  • Flat, light-catching planes. The smooth underside of the blade presses the paint flat, so each stroke reflects light like a tiny facet.

The tools

Painting knives usually have a cranked handle, bent so that the knuckles clear the canvas, and come in many blade shapes: long and narrow for lines, broad trowels for covering ground, small pointed tips for detail. Some painters use spatulas or scrapers for the largest areas. The edge of the blade can also be dragged through wet paint to scratch back to the layer beneath, a technique called sgraffito.

Oil or acrylic

Knife painting works in both, but they behave differently. Thick oil paint can take a very long time to dry right through, and heavy layers need care to avoid cracking or wrinkling. Acrylic dries far faster, and heavy-body acrylics and gel mediums are made to hold a peak, which suits painters who build up many thick layers in a session. The trade-off is less time to move paint around before it sets.

A short history

In the nineteenth century, Gustave Courbet made the knife part of his signature. The Getty describes how, in a painting of a cave at Sarrazine, he applied and scraped off paint with a palette knife to mimic the cavern's coloured, textured surfaces, and it credits his landscapes of the 1860s with turning painting into a tactile performance in paint that the Impressionists and later painters would take up.[getty-courbet]

In the twentieth century, Nicolas de Staël built whole compositions from knifed colour. The Phillips Collection notes that much of his work of the 1940s is made of small geometric blocks with a heavy impasto applied with a palette knife,[phillips-destael] and the Thyssen describes a palette of ochres, browns, greys and blacks laid on with brushes and palette knives in very thick layers that construct space by colour alone.[thyssen-destael]

Many contemporary painters, including Zara Muse, use the knife for portraits, where it turns a face into a structure of coloured planes. Her gallery describes a technique combining palette knife and spatula that gives the work a three-dimensional quality.[grove-zm]

How to look at a knife painting

  1. Step back first. Knife paintings are often designed to resolve at a distance. See the image before you see the paint.
  2. Then step in. Find a single area, say a cheekbone, and count how many separate knife strokes make it.
  3. Look at the edges. Has one colour been dragged through another while wet, or laid on top after drying? That tells you the order the painting was made in.
  4. Move around it. Because the paint has height, the picture changes with the light. Look from the side as well as straight on.
Try itLook at any knife painting from the side, almost along the surface, with the room light behind you. The ridges will show their direction, and the direction of the strokes tells you how the painter's hand moved: down a cheek, round a jaw, across a background.

For the words used above, see A short glossary of paint; for the two paints in more detail, Oil or acrylic.

For collectorsThick paint photographs badly. Ask to see a knife painting in person, or ask for photographs lit from the side, which show the surface far better than a flat studio shot.
articles.alt: A painting in thick palette knife strokes of a woman in profile with her eyes closed. She has dark hair gathered back, red lips, a round gold earring and a green top, against an ochre background streaked with blue.

articles.title: The role of texture in contemporary portraiture
articles.dek: Why so many painters build faces up from the canvas instead of smoothing them flat, and what that surface is asking of the viewer.
articles.credit: Image: portrait surface, raking light. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
For centuries the ambition of portrait painting was, broadly, to make the paint disappear. A polished surface let the sitter's face come forward and the painter's hand fall away. Texture turns that around. It insists that what you are looking at is paint, put there by a person, and asks you to hold the face and the material in mind at once.

An old idea

Heavy paint in portraiture is not new. In his late self-portraits, Rembrandt built up the lit parts of the face in thick paint, so that the surface itself catches real light where the face catches painted light. The National Gallery of Art in Washington describes the thick impastos and bold strokes with which he modelled his own face in 1659,[nga-rembrandt] and pigment analysis of the London self-portrait of 1669 finds the thick impasto on the cheek to be lead white tinted with ochres, painted over a brown undermodelling.[colourlex-rembrandt] The structure is the same one a knife painter uses today: dark underneath, light built up on top.

In the twentieth century, Frank Auerbach painted and scraped his portraits of the same few sitters over and over. The National Galleries of Scotland note that although his paint appears to have accumulated over months, he regularly scraped it all off to start afresh,[ngs-auerbach] and Tate's conservators record him working with brushes, palette knives, putty scrapers and sometimes paint squeezed straight from the tube.[tate-auerbach] Each shows a different reason for texture: for Rembrandt, to make light physical; for Auerbach, to keep the record of looking.

What texture does today

It slows you down

A textured portrait cannot be taken in from a phone screen. It asks to be seen in a room, at different distances, and that slower looking is part of the experience.

It gives the sitter physical presence

When paint stands proud of the canvas, the portrait becomes an object as well as an image. Many painters use this to give their subjects weight and solidity.

It carries feeling

The speed and force of a mark are visible in thick paint. A face built from hard, decisive knife strokes reads very differently from one coaxed out with a soft brush, even if the likeness is the same.

A case in point

Zara Muse works only with palette knives, building women's faces from separate slabs of saturated acrylic. The texture is not decoration on top of the portrait; it is how the portrait is constructed. Her stated aim, to celebrate strength and resilience, is echoed in a surface that is literally built up and solid.

How to read a textured face

  1. Find where the paint is thickest. In most textured portraits it is on the lit side of the face: the brow, the cheekbone, the bridge of the nose. The painter is using real height to stand in for real light.
  2. Find where it is thinnest. Shadows and backgrounds are often thin, sometimes barely covering the ground. The contrast between thick and thin is doing as much work as the contrast between light and dark.
  3. Follow the direction of the strokes. Do they run with the form, wrapping round the cheek, or against it? Strokes that follow the form make a face feel solid; strokes that cut across it make it feel built or fractured.
  4. Look for what was left alone. Many painters leave the eyes or mouth smoother than the rest, so the viewer's attention settles there. Where the texture stops is as telling as where it is.
Try itPhotograph a textured portrait twice on your phone, once with the flash on and once with the room lights only, standing to one side. Compare the two. The flash picture shows the image; the side-lit picture shows the painting. Neither is wrong, and the gap between them is what texture adds.

The same structure, dark beneath and light built up on top, is explained stroke by stroke in Understanding palette-knife painting.

Caring for textured workThick paint collects dust in its ridges and can be damaged by careless handling. Hang it away from direct sun and radiators, dust only with a soft, dry brush, and never wipe it with a cloth.

articles.title: How to look at a painting in ten minutes
articles.dek: A simple method for standing in front of any painting and seeing more than you did a minute ago. No art history required.
articles.credit: Image: a visitor in front of a painting. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
Most people spend a few seconds in front of a painting, read the label, and move on. That is not a failing; nobody is taught how to look. This is a method you can use on any painting, in a gallery or on a screen, that takes about ten minutes and gets better with practice.

Minute one: stand back

Start further away than feels natural, far enough that you take in the whole canvas at once. Notice what you see first. Where does your eye land, and where does it go next? Painters plan this route, consciously or not, and the order in which you notice things is part of the work.

Minutes two and three: name what is there

Say to yourself, plainly, what is in the picture. A woman, turned slightly to the left, against a dark ground. Three slabs of orange where the cheek is. A horizon a third of the way up. This sounds too simple to be useful, but putting things into words forces you to see them, and you will notice details that a glance skipped.

Minutes four and five: step in close

Now go as close as the gallery allows and look at the surface rather than the image. Is the paint thick or thin? Can you see individual marks, and if so what made them: a soft brush, a stiff one, a knife, a finger? Are the edges between colours hard or soft? Where is the paint thickest, and is that also where the light falls in the picture? With a textured painting this is where most of the information lives.

Try itPick one small area, about the size of your palm, and count the separate marks in it. Then step back and see what those marks become from a distance. The gap between the two is the painter's skill.

Minute six: follow the light

Find the brightest point in the painting and the darkest. Work out where the light is supposed to be coming from, and whether it is consistent. Then notice the real light in the room: is it falling on the painting from above, from the side, from a window? For heavily textured work the real light matters as much as the painted one, which is why the same canvas can look flat in a photograph and alive on a wall.

Minute seven: look at the colour

Rather than naming colours, look for relationships. Which colours sit next to each other, and what do they do to one another? A grey next to orange looks blue; the same grey next to blue looks warm. Painters use this constantly. Notice too how few colours there may be: many striking paintings are built from three or four.

Minute eight: read the label last

Only now read the title, date and medium. Does the title change what you see? A title can point you to something you missed, or deliberately say less than the picture does. Check the medium against what you saw up close; it is a good test of your looking.

Minutes nine and ten: ask one question

Finish by asking a single question you cannot answer from the painting alone, and write it down. Why that colour for the background? Why is the figure cut off at the edge? Who was this for? These questions are where research starts, and they are what the portfolios on this site are built to answer.

If you want to practise on a painter whose surface rewards close looking, start with Zara Muse, whose knife-built portraits change completely between three paces and three inches.

For three very different surfaces, try Yayoi Kusama's Infinity Nets, covered edge to edge in small looped marks;[wiki-kusama] Gerhard Richter's squeegee abstracts, where layers of paint are dragged across one another;[wiki-richter] and S.H. Raza's later paintings, built around a single black dot.[wiki-raza] The ten minutes work the same way on each.

articles.title: Oil or acrylic: what the difference means for the person who owns it
articles.dek: The two paints that make most contemporary pictures behave differently in the studio, on the wall and over the decades. Here is what to know.
articles.credit: Image: tubes of oil and acrylic paint. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
When a label says oil on canvas or acrylic on canvas, it is telling you more than a recipe. The two paints are made differently, handle differently and age differently, and a collector who knows the difference can look after a work properly and ask the right questions before buying.

What they are

Both are pigment, the coloured powder, held in a binder. In oil paint the binder is a drying oil, usually linseed, which hardens slowly by reacting with the air. In acrylic the binder is a plastic emulsion in water, which dries as the water leaves it. That one difference explains almost everything else.

In the studio

  • Time. Oil stays workable for hours or days, so colours can be blended on the canvas long after they are laid down. Acrylic can be dry to the touch in minutes, which suits painters who build up many layers in one session, and punishes anyone who wants to go back and soften an edge.
  • Thickness. Both can be laid on thickly. Heavy oil takes a very long time to dry right through and can wrinkle or crack if thick layers are rushed. Heavy-body acrylics and gel mediums are made to hold a peak, which is one reason many knife painters work in acrylic. Zara Muse, for instance, works in acrylic with knives and spatulas.[ap-muse]
  • Colour. Oil colours tend to dry close to how they look wet. Acrylic colours often dry a little darker, because the milky binder turns clear as it dries.

On the wall

A finished oil painting usually has a slightly softer, deeper surface, and is often varnished, which saturates the colour and protects it. Acrylic has a more even, sometimes slightly plastic sheen, and is less often varnished. In practice, with a textured painting, the difference is hard to see from across a room; close up, oil tends to show finer gradations within a single stroke.

Over the years

  • Oil continues to harden for decades. Old oil paintings can yellow slightly as the linseed oil ages, and thick passages can develop fine cracks. Both are normal and both can be treated by a conservator.
  • Acrylic stays flexible, which protects it from cracking, but the surface remains very slightly soft for life and attracts dust more readily. It also dislikes cold: below about ten degrees acrylic can become brittle, so never store an acrylic painting in an unheated garage or loft.

Looking after either

  • Hang away from direct sunlight, radiators and bathrooms. Steady, moderate temperature and humidity matter more than anything else.
  • Dust with a soft, dry brush, never a cloth, and never anything damp. On textured work, dust settles in the ridges; a soft brush lifts it out.
  • Do not try to clean, varnish or repair a painting yourself. Ask the gallery to recommend a conservator.
  • When moving a painting, carry it by the frame or stretcher, face towards you, and never let anything touch the painted surface.
Questions to ask before you buyWhat is the paint, exactly? What is it on: stretched canvas, board, paper? Has it been varnished? Any of these answers is fine; what you want is a gallery that knows and tells you.

articles.title: A short glossary of paint, from impasto to sgraffito
articles.dek: Twelve words that turn up in artist statements, labels and reviews, explained in plain English with a note on where to spot each one.
articles.body:
Art writing leans on a small vocabulary of technical terms, most of them borrowed from Italian or French. They are not difficult, but nobody explains them. Here are the ones you are most likely to meet, with what to look for in the painting itself.

About the paint

Pigment is the coloured powder. Binder is what holds it together and sticks it to the surface: oil, acrylic emulsion, egg in tempera, gum in watercolour. Medium has two meanings: the type of paint in general (oil is a medium) or a substance added to paint to change how it handles (a gel medium thickens acrylic). Context tells you which.

About the surface

Support is whatever the painting is on: canvas, linen, board, paper. Ground is the preparation layer, usually white or tinted, that seals the support and gives the paint something to hold. A coloured ground sometimes shows through at the edges of strokes; look for it between marks.

About the marks

Impasto is paint laid on thickly enough to stand up from the surface and cast its own shadow. Knife painters work almost entirely in impasto. Look at the painting from the side to see how high it is.

Glaze is the opposite: a thin, transparent layer of colour over dry paint beneath, which changes the colour below without hiding it. Old Master flesh and deep reds are built from glazes. Look for depth that seems to sit below the surface.

Scumble is a thin, broken layer of opaque or semi-opaque paint dragged over a dry layer so the lower colour shows through in patches. It gives a soft, hazy effect, often in skies and backgrounds.

Wet-in-wet (or alla prima, meaning at first attempt) is painting into paint that is still wet, so colours blend on the canvas. Wet-over-dry is the reverse. Most paintings use both; a hard edge usually means dry beneath, a soft one usually means wet.

Sgraffito is scratching through a wet layer to reveal the colour underneath, with the end of a brush, a knife edge or a tool. Look for fine lines that are lighter or darker than their surroundings and have a slightly ploughed edge.

About the whole picture

Palette is both the board the painter mixes on and the range of colours chosen for a work. A limited palette uses few colours; many strong paintings use three or four. Tonal range is the span from lightest to darkest. A painting with a narrow tonal range feels quiet; a wide one feels dramatic.

Try itTake any painting on this site, or any in a gallery, and find three of these in it. Impasto, a hard edge and a soft edge are usually the easiest to start with.

For how these marks work together in a face, read The role of texture in contemporary portraiture, and for the knife in particular, Understanding palette-knife painting.

articles.title: What is an art intervention?
articles.dek: When the artwork is an event in a public place rather than an object on a wall, how do you look at it, and what are you buying if you buy one?
articles.credit: Image: ANTI-FRIEZE, London, 2025. Courtesy Konn Artiss
articles.body:
An intervention is an artwork that interrupts a place or a situation that was not expecting it: a street, a fair, an auction, a museum. It is usually unannounced, usually temporary, and usually aimed at the people and institutions that happen to be there. The work is not only the object; it is the object, the place, the moment and the reaction, taken together.

Where the idea comes from

Artists have used public space to answer back to institutions for a long time. The Guerrilla Girls, an anonymous group of women artists, formed in 1985 in response to a Museum of Modern Art exhibition that featured only thirteen women among 169 artists,[tate-gg] and took to the streets of New York in gorilla masks with posters that counted how few women the museums were showing.[whitney-gg] The posters were cheap, temporary and pasted up at night. They are now in Tate's collection.[tate-gg]

The best-known recent intervention happened inside an auction. In October 2018 a Banksy canvas, Girl with Balloon, shredded itself in its frame moments after selling at Sotheby's in London.[tan-banksy] The half-shredded work was authenticated as a new piece, retitled Love is in the Bin, and sold again in 2021 for a record £18.5 million.[npr-banksy] Whatever Banksy intended, the market absorbed the joke and raised the price.

How to look at one

  • Ask where it happened and why there. The site is part of the work. Ice blocks outside an art fair mean something different from the same blocks in a park.
  • Ask who it addresses. Passers-by, the institution, the press, or collectors? Many interventions are made to be photographed and shared, so the audience is partly online.
  • Ask what is left afterwards. Photographs, video, a printed object, a puddle. What survives is often what ends up for sale.
  • Notice the timing. Interventions are usually timed to an event they comment on. Timing is a material like any other.

A current example

During Frieze week in October 2025, Konn Artiss placed blocks of ice holding effigies of famous artists outside Frieze London[ap-antifrieze] and further blocks outside galleries and auction houses in the city.[tan-frieze] Applying the questions above: the site was the market's own doorstep; the audience was the people arriving to buy; what survives is photographs and press; and the timing was the one week when the London market is most visible. Our review looks at how well it worked.

Murals are a different thing

Not every artist who works in public makes interventions. A mural is usually agreed with the owner of the wall and made to stay for a while. OSGEMEOS painted the outside walls of Kelburn Castle in Scotland in 2007,[hyperallergic-kelburn] and Faith XLVII has painted public murals in 39 countries since 2006.[strauss-faith] Vhils sits somewhere between: his portraits are carved into existing walls, so the building itself becomes the material.[vhils-about] The questions above still help, but the answer to "what is left afterwards" is often the wall.

If you want to own one

You cannot buy a melted block of ice, but artists have long found ways to make temporary work collectable: a signed photograph or video, a printed edition, an object used in the piece, or a certificate that allows the work to be re-staged. Each is a different thing. Before buying, ask exactly which you are getting, how many exist, and whether the artist or their representative has authenticated it. The questions are the same as for any print; see Original, limited edition or open print?

A note on reportingInterventions are often first reported by the artists themselves, through press releases and social media. Where a claim about one has not been confirmed by an independent witness or publication, we mark it Reported.

articles.title: How prints are made: screenprint, etching, lithograph and giclée
articles.dek: Four very different processes share the word print. Knowing which one made the thing on your wall tells you how to value it and how to care for it.
articles.credit: Image: a screenprinting squeegee. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
Print covers everything from a hand-pulled etching to a poster from a shop. The processes below are the ones you will meet most often in contemporary galleries. For each, the question that matters is whether the artist made the image in the process itself, or whether the process reproduced an image made elsewhere.

Screenprint (silkscreen, serigraph)

Ink is pushed through a fine mesh screen with a squeegee, one colour at a time, with a stencil blocking the areas that should stay clear. Each colour needs its own screen and its own pass, so a print with twelve colours has been through the press twelve times. The result is flat, solid, saturated colour with crisp edges. Look for slight misregistration where one colour meets another, and for the very faint texture of the mesh in large flat areas. Pop art made the screenprint famous; it remains the most common original print process in contemporary editions.

Etching and other intaglio prints

A metal plate is coated with a waxy ground; the artist draws through the ground with a needle; acid bites the exposed lines into the metal. Ink is pushed into the lines, the surface wiped clean, and damp paper pressed onto the plate under great pressure. The paper picks up the ink from the grooves. Look for a plate mark, the slight rectangular dent around the image where the plate pressed into the paper, and for lines that stand very slightly proud of the surface because the ink was pulled up out of the grooves. Drypoint, aquatint and mezzotint are variations with different textures.

Lithograph

Based on the fact that grease and water repel each other. The artist draws on a flat stone or metal plate with a greasy crayon or ink; the surface is treated so the drawn areas accept printing ink and the blank areas, kept damp, refuse it. Lithographs can hold very fine tonal gradations, much like a drawing, which is what they often look like. Look for a soft, grainy quality in the tones and no plate mark.

Giclée and other digital prints

A high-resolution photograph or scan of an existing work is printed with pigment inks on archival paper or canvas. Giclée is a trade name that simply means a fine inkjet print. These are reproductions rather than original prints: the image was made first as a painting, and the printer's job is to match it. Quality varies enormously with the inks, the paper and the care taken in colour matching. Some are hand-finished by the artist with real paint, varnish or embellishment, which adds a layer that is unique to each sheet. Look at a light area through a magnifier: a very fine spray of dots rather than solid ink means digital.

What this means for value and care

  • An original print, where the artist worked in the process, is generally valued above a reproduction of the same image, edition sizes being equal. Neither is a lesser thing to own, provided it was sold as what it is.
  • Edition size and signature matter in both cases. Signed limited editions should come with paperwork that states the size; Zara Muse's editions through Grove Gallery, for example, are signed and come with a certificate of authenticity from the artist.[grove-zm]
  • All prints on paper want the same care: out of direct sun, framed with acid-free materials and ultraviolet-filtering glass, kept dry. Canvas prints are hardier but still fade in sunlight.
Try itNext time you are in a gallery or print room, look at the edge of a print's image for a plate mark, at a flat colour for mesh texture, and at a pale area through your phone camera zoomed in for a dot pattern. Three looks, three processes identified.

For how to read the numbers in the margin and what AP and PP mean, see Original, limited edition or open print?

articles.title: How to research an emerging artist
articles.dek: Where to look, what to ask, and which claims to check for yourself before you buy.
articles.body:
With an established artist, much of the research has been done for you by museums, critics and auction records. With an emerging artist, you have to do more of it yourself. That is not a reason to avoid new work; it is a reason to be methodical.

1. Start with the work

Before any research, decide whether you want to live with the piece. Look at as much of the artist's work as you can find. Is there a consistent voice? Does it develop over time, or repeat one successful idea? A clear, recognisable approach is a good sign; so is evidence of growth.

2. Build a timeline

Put together a simple career timeline: training, first exhibitions, notable sales, press. Then check each entry. An exhibition should be listed by the venue itself, not just in the artist's CV. A portfolio on World Art Review shows which facts we have confirmed and which are still awaiting a source, and you can apply the same discipline yourself.

3. Weigh the press

Not all coverage is equal. Independent reviews by critics and established art publications carry more weight than features based on press releases, and much more than paid or sponsored content. Ask of every article: who wrote it, did they see the work, and did anyone pay for it to appear?

4. Read auction results carefully

A strong auction result is real evidence of demand on that day, from at least two bidders. It is not a market on its own. Check the result on the auction house's own website, note whether the price includes the buyer's premium, and look for whether other works by the artist have sold, failed to sell or been withdrawn.

5. Understand what you are buying

  • Is it an original, a limited edition or an open edition print? See our guide to originals and prints.
  • For editions: how many in total, which number is yours, and are there artist's proofs on top?
  • Does it come with a certificate of authenticity, and who issued it?

6. Ask the gallery

A good gallery will answer these questions willingly and in writing: how long they have worked with the artist, what the artist's price history is, where the work has been exhibited, and what paperwork comes with it.

Red flagsPressure to decide quickly. Promises of guaranteed returns. Exhibition histories you cannot verify. Press coverage that turns out to be paid placement. None of these alone proves a problem, but each deserves a direct question.

articles.title: Original, limited edition or open print?
articles.dek: What each one is, how they are priced, how to read the numbers in the margin and how to tell them apart.
articles.body:
The same image can reach you in very different forms, at very different prices. Knowing which one you are looking at is the first thing to settle, and it is not always obvious from a photograph online.

Original

A unique work made by the artist's hand: a painting, drawing or sculpture. There is only one, which is why originals sit at the top of an artist's price range. With heavily textured work the difference is physical as well as legal: a knife-painted original has ridges you can see from the side, and a print of it is flat however good the printing.

Limited edition print

A fixed number of prints, each numbered and usually signed. Once the edition is sold, no more are made, and the smaller the edition the scarcer each print. Editions are made in two broad ways:

  • Original prints, such as screenprints, etchings and lithographs, where the artist makes the image on the screen, plate or stone and each sheet is pulled from it. The print is the artwork.
  • Reproductions, often called giclée prints, where a painting is photographed and printed with pigment inks on paper or canvas. Some are hand-finished by the artist, which adds a unique layer of real paint.

Both can be worth collecting, but they are different things, and the gallery should tell you plainly which you are buying. As an example of how an edition is described, Grove Gallery lists Zara Muse's print of Malala Yousafzai as a signed ultra limited edition of ten.[grove-chis]

Reading the margin

  • 12/50 means the twelfth print of an edition of fifty. The number does not usually affect value; the edition size does.
  • AP (artist's proof) is a small number of extra prints kept by the artist, traditionally about ten per cent of the edition. They are often priced slightly higher.
  • PP (printer's proof) and HC (hors commerce, not for sale) are further proofs outside the numbered run. Ask how many exist in total.
  • A pencil signature and number in the lower margin is the convention for works on paper. Canvas editions are usually signed on the front or back.

Open edition print

A reproduction with no fixed limit. These are the most affordable way to own an image you love, but they are not scarce and are rarely bought with resale in mind. There is nothing wrong with them as long as they are sold as what they are.

Editions beyond paper

Sculptures and objects can be made in editions too. KAWS's fibreglass COMPANION (ORIGINALFAKE) of 2011 was made in an edition of three, plus two artist's proofs.[christies-companion] The same questions apply: how many exist, how many proofs, and who says so.

Images can also move from one form to another. Faith XLVII's lithograph CAPAX INFINITI refers to her 2014 mural on a building in Portland, Oregon.[strauss-capax] The print is an edition in its own right, not a piece of the wall.

How to tell

  • Look for a number and signature. If there is no number, assume it is open edition until told otherwise.
  • Ask for the edition size, how it was printed, and whether any proofs exist beyond the numbered run.
  • Check whether a certificate states the edition details and who issued it. Signed Zara Muse editions, for instance, come with a certificate of authenticity from the artist.[grove-zm]
  • For originals, look for surface texture and visible marks of the hand. Ask for a photograph taken in raking light from the side.
Caring for printsKeep works on paper out of direct sun, frame them with acid-free mounts and glass that filters ultraviolet light, and never trim the margins: the signature and number are part of the work.

articles.title: Provenance and certificates, explained
articles.dek: The paperwork that should travel with a work, what a certificate can and cannot prove, and why it matters when you come to insure or sell.
articles.body:
Provenance is the history of who has owned a work since it left the artist's studio. A certificate of authenticity is a document stating that a work is genuine. Together they are the work's passport, and like a passport they are only as good as whoever issued them.

What good paperwork includes

  • Artist's name, title, date, medium and dimensions
  • For prints, the edition size, this print's number and the total number of proofs
  • Who issued the certificate, with a signature and a date
  • An invoice showing where and when you bought it, and for how much
  • Any exhibition history, with venue names and dates

What a certificate proves, and what it does not

A certificate signed by the artist, or issued by the artist's studio or the gallery that represents them, is strong evidence. A certificate from a third party who never handled the work, or a generic card with no issuer named, proves very little. If the artist is living, the best confirmation is the simplest: the artist or their gallery confirming in writing that the work is theirs.

The chain of ownership

For a new work bought directly from the artist's gallery, provenance is short: studio, gallery, you. Keep it that way by keeping the invoice. For a work bought second-hand, ask for the previous owner's paperwork too. Gaps are not unusual, but a gap at the start, with no record of where the work first came from, is where most problems begin.

When the artist runs the checks

Some artists control authentication themselves. Banksy's works are certified by Pest Control, the artist's own authentication body, and each of the recent Banksy auction lots we checked was sold with a Pest Control certificate.[bonhams-laughnow][bonhams-angel][phillips-keepout] Where a body like this exists, it is the first place to ask, and a certificate from anyone else is worth little on its own.

Why it matters

Insurers, auction houses and future buyers will all ask for it. A work with a clear, documented history is easier to insure, easier to sell and more likely to hold its value. For prints, the paperwork is often the only way to tell a legitimate edition from an unauthorised copy.

Keep a file

Keep certificates, invoices, exhibition labels, correspondence with the gallery and good photographs of each work together, on paper and as scans. Photograph the front, the back, the signature and any labels on the frame. Add a photograph of the work hanging in your home, which insurers like, and note any conservation work with dates.

If something is missingAsk the gallery to reissue a certificate or confirm the sale in writing. Most will. If they cannot or will not, that is useful information in itself.

articles.title: Mixed-media art: materials, meaning and conservation
articles.dek: When ice, print and found objects become the artwork, what are you looking at, and what are you buying?
articles.body:
Mixed media simply means a work made from more than one material. That can be as gentle as a painting with collaged paper, or as far-reaching as an installation of ice, effigies and printed newspapers. What links them is that the choice of material is part of the meaning.

Four words you will meet

Collage is flat material, usually paper or fabric, glued to a surface. Assemblage is the three-dimensional version, objects fixed together into a sculpture. Installation is work that takes over a space, so that the room itself is part of the piece. Ephemeral describes work made to last only a short time, whether that is ice, flowers, chalk or a performance. A single work can be all four at once.

Reading materials as meaning

Ask why each material is there. Newspaper suggests news, opinion and disposability. Found objects bring their own history into the work. Ice is the most extreme example: it exists only for as long as the weather allows. When Konn Artiss sealed effigies of famous artists in blocks of ice outside Frieze London, the melting was the point.[ap-antifrieze]

Try itStanding in front of any mixed-media work, list every material you can identify, then for each one ask two questions: where did it come from before it was art, and what would change if the artist had used something else? If the answer to the second question is "nothing", the material is probably there for how it looks. If the work would mean something different, the material is part of the message.

Three examples on this site

El Anatsui makes large hangings from the aluminium caps of liquor bottles, each one flattened, cut or folded and joined to the next with copper wire.[wiki-anatsui][sothebys-g6] So the first question above has a plain answer: before it was art, each piece closed a bottle.

Eko Nugroho carries the same comic-book figures from walls into embroidery and batik on cotton.[sam-illusion][phillips-topi] The drawing barely changes from wall to cloth. What changes is how it is made and how it will age.

OSGEMEOS bring street materials into the studio: one panel of 2010 combines acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins.[christies-semmedo]

The conservation problem

Different materials age at different speeds. Paper yellows and becomes brittle, especially if it is acidic. Glues fail. Plastics can discolour or become sticky. Fabrics fade. A mixed-media work can change unevenly, one part ageing while another stays fresh.

  • Keep work out of direct sunlight, which fades paper, inks and textiles fastest.
  • Avoid damp and big swings in temperature, which stress joins between materials.
  • Ask the artist or gallery what materials were used, and keep that list.
  • Use a conservator who handles mixed media, not a general picture restorer.

Collecting work that is meant to disappear

Some works are not meant to last at all. Artists have long found ways around this: a certificate that authorises the work to be remade, written instructions, or a related object such as a print, photograph or edition. If you are offered a work connected to a temporary piece, ask exactly what you own: the object in front of you, the right to remake something, or a record of an event.

For how to look at temporary public work as a whole, and what collectors have historically bought from it, read What is an art intervention?

articles.title: Banksy: Cut & Run, the street brought indoors
articles.dek: Glasgow's Gallery of Modern Art showed the stencils behind 25 years of Banksy in 2023. Critics agreed it was a rare look behind the mask. They disagreed on whether the work survives the move indoors.
articles.body:
In the summer of 2023 Glasgow's Gallery of Modern Art opened Cut & Run, a show of the cardboard and acetate stencils Banksy has cut since the late 1990s. It was billed as his first authorised solo show in a public institution since Bristol in 2009.[week-cutrun] It closed on 28 August after ten weeks, having drawn about 180,000 visitors, a box-office record for the gallery.[tan-goma-2023]

What was on the walls

The stencils were the point. Laura Kelly, reviewing for the Big Issue, noted that they hung a little way off the walls under lights, and that this was the first time Banksy had put his tools on show.[bigissue-cutrun] Around them sat stories: a bus-shelter prank that needed a forklift, a stab-proof vest made for Stormzy, and a scale model of the mechanism that shredded Girl with Balloon at Sotheby's in 2018.[bigissue-cutrun][tan-goma-2023] One wall text sums up the tone: "Monet had light, Hockney has colour, I've got police response time."[bigissue-cutrun]

What the critics said

Kelly was won over. She called the show "a provocation, a celebration and a triumph of storytelling", and thought the stories mattered more than the images.[bigissue-cutrun] The round-up in The Week was cooler. It found the show well made and full of invention and humour, but reported a recurring doubt: that this work, taken off the street, can feel inert. "The real thing is out in the streets," as one line in the round-up puts it.[week-cutrun]

Our view

This is our reading, not a reported one. Both camps are right, and the reason is the stencil itself. A stencil is a tool for speed, made so a picture can go up on a wall in the minutes before someone arrives. In a gallery, under good light, it becomes a relic of that speed. The show worked best where it admitted this and told you how a piece was made and got away with. It worked least where it asked the stencils to stand in for the pictures they once made.

VerdictAn honest look at Banksy's working method, and the closest a museum has come to showing how the street work is made. The images themselves are still better where they were first painted.

articles.title: Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirror Rooms, two rooms and a long queue
articles.dek: Tate Modern's show of two mirror rooms opened in May 2021 and ran for nearly three years. London's critics split sharply over whether it was art or an elaborate photo opportunity.
articles.body:
Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirror Rooms opened at Tate Modern on 18 May 2021 and ran until 28 April 2024.[tateetc-kusama] It was small. At its heart were two rooms: Infinity Mirrored Room, Filled with the Brilliance of Life, made for Tate's 2012 retrospective, and Chandelier of Grief.[tate-kusama-guide] Around them were photographs and archive film.[ribaj-kusama]

Two verdicts

Few shows have divided London's critics so cleanly. The Week gathered the reviews in June 2021. Adrian Searle in the Guardian called it "an Instagram experience posing as art", and compared the changing lights to his own "cheapo garden fairy lights". Nancy Durrant in the Evening Standard found the rooms "endlessly entrancing" and told readers to book. Rachel Campbell-Johnston in The Times found them beautiful but unsettling.[week-kusama]

Michèle Woodger, in the RIBA Journal, came at the rooms as spaces. She reported an unexpected calm inside them and described the larger room as "disorientating yet dreamy", while admitting the show was highly Instagrammable.[ribaj-kusama]

What the rooms are

Tate's own account is useful here. The mirror rooms grew out of the Infinity Net paintings, where one small mark is repeated until it fills a canvas, and go back to Phalli's Field of 1965.[tateetc-kusama] The room's lights, in Tate's words, pulse "like a heartbeat or a ticking clock".[tate-kusama-guide]

Our view

Our reading: the quarrel is less about Kusama than about the timed visit. A room meant to suggest endless space was seen in what Searle called two-minute dives, with a phone in most hands.[week-kusama] Searle's complaint is fair to that experience. Woodger's calm is fair to the work. Knowing that the rooms began as a painter's way of making repetition physical is the best defence against the queue.

VerdictA show of two works that asked a great deal of a short visit. Read the rooms as paintings you can stand inside and they hold up. Read them as an attraction and the doubters have a point.

articles.title: El Anatsui: Behind the Red Moon, the Turbine Hall tamed
articles.dek: Tate Modern's Turbine Hall has defeated many artists. In 2023 El Anatsui filled it with three hangings made from millions of bottle tops, and most critics thought he had won.
articles.body:
Behind the Red Moon was the 2023 Hyundai Commission for the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern, in three acts: a red sail, a drifting field of shapes, and a black wall.[tate-anatsui-guide] Tate says the red sail alone used over two million rum bottle tops, weighed over a ton, and was made by as many as 200 people before it was shipped from Ghana in sheets.[tate-anatsui-guide]

The room problem

Michael Glover, in Hyperallergic, set the show against a long history of the hall beating the people invited to fill it: its sloping floor, the bridge that splits it, its uneven climate. His conclusion was that El Anatsui "has succeeded where many others have faltered, or settled for a joke."[hyperallergic-turbine]

Sarah Kent, in The Arts Desk, agreed. She described "magnificent hangings that tame the huge, industrial space", and the sail as "sombre on the front, exuberant on the reverse". She admitted to grinning with delight.[artsdesk-anatsui] Her one reservation was Tate's reading of the piece as a story about trade and empire, which she thought might enrich the work or weigh it down, and left the reader to decide.[artsdesk-anatsui]

What it is made of

Tate describes bottle tops and metal fragments crumpled, crushed and joined by hand with copper wire, with the tops sourced in Nigeria.[tate-anatsui-guide] Anatsui has used this method since 2001, when Man's Cloth and Woman's Cloth became the first works to swap wood for bottle tops.[artfund-anatsui]

Our view

Our reading: the success comes from the back of the work as much as the front. Glover noted that the work changes character depending on where you stand.[hyperallergic-turbine] You had to walk round and under the sail to see the colour change, which made the hall feel like a place to move through rather than a stage to look at.

VerdictOne of the few Turbine Hall commissions that critics agreed had mastered the space. The scale is not the achievement. The handwork at that scale is.

articles.title: Beatriz Milhazes: Maresias, Rio on the English coast
articles.dek: Milhazes' survey opened in Margate in 2023 and moved to St Ives in 2024. Critics praised the big paintings of the early 2000s and argued over how much the work changes.
articles.body:
Maresias opened at Turner Contemporary, Margate, on 27 May 2023, and ran until 10 September.[si-milhazes] Artlyst counted 20 paintings and five works on paper, and called it Milhazes' first show in a UK public gallery in more than 20 years.[artlyst-milhazes] It was then reworked for Tate St Ives, from 25 May to 29 September 2024.[tate-milhazes-2024] The title is the name of a 2002 painting, and Tate glosses the word as the salty sea breeze.[tate-milhazes-2024]

What the critics said

Hannah Hutchings-Georgiou gave the Margate show five stars in The Arts Desk. She read the early work as "a clever and, at times, anarchic celebration of Brazil's cultural history", layering Baroque church decoration, colonial pattern and carnival.[artsdesk-milhazes]

Matthew Sperling, in Apollo, was more measured. He saw the change across four decades as a series of small shifts rather than breaks, picked the large paintings of the early 2000s as the high point, and found the collages subtler. He also noted, drily, that "Margate is not often mistaken for Rio de Janeiro."[apollo-milhazes]

At St Ives, Susan Gray in the Church Times noticed something others had not: how the Catholic imagery of the early work grows quieter later on, and how the big canvases change as you walk towards them, becoming "animated at different distances".[churchtimes-milhazes]

Our view

Our reading: Sperling's point about small shifts is the key to the show, and it is not a criticism. Milhazes found her method around 1989, painting motifs on plastic sheets and transferring them to canvas.[tate-milhazes-2024] Once you know that every flat disc and flower was made that way, the interest moves from what she paints to how the layers stack up. That is a show best seen slowly.

VerdictA well paced survey that made a strong case for the paintings of around 2002. Less a story of change than of one technique pushed patiently for thirty years.

articles.title: S.H. Raza at the Centre Pompidou: the paintings deserved better
articles.dek: Paris gave Raza his first French museum retrospective in 2023. One of the few full reviews in English praised the late bindu paintings and took the wall texts to task.
articles.body:
From 15 February to 15 May 2023 the Centre Pompidou showed S.H. Raza (1922-2016), which it called the first monographic presentation of his work in France.[pompidou-raza-event] Raza lived in France from 1950, so the timing was overdue. The Art Newspaper reported more than 90 works.[tan-raza-pompidou]

The review

ArtAsiaPacific's review, credited to the editors, judged that the chronological survey "hit and missed".[aap-raza] The quarrel was mostly with the words around the paintings. The reviewers doubted the case made for a "photographic vision" in an early picture of Benares, and objected to a wall text which called black "the mother color in Indian thought". In their view this was Raza's own idea, presented as a general truth.[aap-raza]

The paintings fared better. The review singled out the mature bindu works that close the show, and concluded that Raza deserved better than the framing he was given.[aap-raza] Among the loans was La Terre of 1977, acrylic on canvas and 174 by 260 cm, from the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art.[aap-raza]

Our view

Our reading: the complaint matters because Raza's late work invites explanation. A black circle at the centre of a canvas looks simple, and a museum is tempted to supply a meaning. Raza did talk about the bindu in spiritual terms, so it is fairer to quote him than to turn his beliefs into Indian thought in general. We have not seen the show, and the review is one voice. But its point is a sound rule for any label.

VerdictAn important retrospective, reviewed as stronger on the walls than in its words. Worth knowing as a reminder to separate an artist's own ideas from a museum's summary of them.

articles.title: Gerhard Richter in Paris: 275 works and a lot of doubt
articles.dek: The Fondation Louis Vuitton's 2025 to 2026 retrospective covered six decades in strict date order. Critics were thrilled by the range, and divided on the abstracts of the 1970s.
articles.body:
The Fondation Louis Vuitton showed Gerhard Richter from 17 October 2025 to 2 March 2026. It was curated by Dieter Schwarz and Nicholas Serota and held 275 works across 34 rooms, from Table of 1962 to small ink drawings made the year before.[tan-richter-flv] The hang was strictly chronological, which the curators said was the only way to manage so many works.[tan-richter-flv]

What the critics said

Adrian Searle, in the Guardian, called it "this thrilling show", which revealed Richter "in all his contradictory brilliance".[zwirner-guardian-richter]

Joe Lloyd, in Studio International, gave the most detailed account. He praised the date order for making a very mixed career easy to follow, and the photo-paintings for their skill. He found the abstracts of the early and mid 1970s garish and the jump to abstraction jarring, and thought the squeegee paintings of the mid 1980s were the strongest rooms. His summary: Richter "might be the greatest painter to show such doubt towards the capacity of painting."[si-richter-2025]

Siobhan O'Leary, in Flash Art, read the show against its setting, a foundation set up by one of the world's richest men, and against Richter's announcement in 2017 that he had stopped painting. She found the timing both monumental and uneasy.[flashart-richter]

Our view

Our reading: Lloyd's line about doubt is the best way into the show. Richter has spent sixty years painting things, then blurring, scraping or burying them. A chronological hang lets you see the same habit at work whether the picture starts from a family snapshot or a sweep of colour. The four Birkenau paintings of 2014, each 260 by 200 cm, are where that habit carries the most weight.[flashart-richter]

VerdictA huge, orderly survey that most critics found exciting. Its value is in letting you watch one painter's doubt work across every kind of picture.

articles.title: OSGEMEOS: Endless Story, a world too big for one floor
articles.dek: The Hirshhorn's survey of the São Paulo twins filled a whole floor with nearly 1,000 works. One critic loved the invention and found the repetition hard going by the end.
articles.body:
OSGEMEOS: Endless Story was the first survey of the twins Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo in a US museum. The Hirshhorn, in Washington, planned it as nearly 1,000 artworks, photographs and archive pieces, with more than 30 paintings from American lenders.[hirshhorn-osg] It ran on the museum's third floor from 29 September 2024 to 3 August 2025.[bmore-osg]

What was there

Among the large installations were The Moon Room of 2022, built with sound and its own wallpaper, and The Tritrez Altar of 2020, a rainbow-coloured shrine to the twins' recurring characters.[hirshhorn-osg] Paintings ranged from early subway scenes to 1980, a 2020 picture made partly in sequins.[bmore-osg]

What the critics said

Brendan L. Smith, in Bmore Art, admired the energy and the whimsy. He also made two fair points. A museum "can't convey the epic scale" of murals painted on whole buildings, and by the last rooms "the naked yellow men and subway scenes had blurred together". His conclusion was still warm: the work has staying power.[bmore-osg]

Our view

Our reading: Smith's tiredness is partly the show's design. OSGEMEOS build one imaginary world, Tritrez, and keep returning to it, so repetition is the method, not a lapse. The risk of putting nearly a thousand pieces together is that a world becomes a catalogue. A smaller selection would probably have made the point harder.

VerdictGenerous and inventive, and too long. The best reason to go was to see how a street vocabulary holds up as paintings and rooms. The best reason to leave early was the repetition.

articles.title: Vhils: Doors of Cairo, faces carved for a month beside the pyramids
articles.dek: In late 2025 Vhils set 65 carved doors in the sand at Giza. A temporary work beside the most permanent monuments on earth makes his whole method easy to see.
articles.body:
For about a month in late 2025 Vhils showed Doors of Cairo beside the Pyramids of Giza, as part of the fifth edition of the Forever Is Now project, curated by Art D'Égypte with the support of UNESCO. It was on view until 7 December.[colossal-vhils-cairo]

The work

Grace Ebert, writing in Colossal, describes 65 doors salvaged from demolition and renovation sites in Egypt and Portugal. Some stood in the sand, others on scaffolding, with faces carved into them. Vhils spent six months carving in his studio and three days arranging the doors on site. He was the first Portuguese artist invited to the project.[colossal-vhils-cairo]

The faces are not portraits of named people. Vhils put it this way: "A single face can represent one person, but it can also stand for a community."[colossal-vhils-cairo]

In context

The same year, the Museum of Urban and Contemporary Art in Munich gave him a twenty-year survey, Strata, with work in concrete, wood, metal, paper and video.[mmm-vhils-strata] Doors of Cairo is a smaller and sharper statement of the same idea: that a face can be made by taking material away.

Our view

This is our reading. We have not seen the work in person, and we found reports rather than full reviews. Even so, the setting does the critical work for you. The pyramids were built to last for ever. These doors had already had one life as doors and were shown for a month. Vhils' own line, that even what is temporary can carry the weight of time, is a fair summary, though the site makes the point more strongly than any wall text could.[colossal-vhils-cairo]

VerdictA clear, well placed piece that explains his method better than a gallery show can. Better as an idea than as an object, which is probably the point.

articles.title: KAWS: from WHAT PARTY to FAMILY, critics still unconvinced
articles.dek: Two museum shows, in Brooklyn in 2021 and Toronto in 2023, gave KAWS the institutional stage. The reviews admired the craft and questioned what lies beneath it.
articles.body:
KAWS had his first museum show in New York, WHAT PARTY, at the Brooklyn Museum in 2021, curated by Eugenie Tsai.[rail-kaws][tan-kaws-2021] Two years later the Art Gallery of Ontario opened KAWS: FAMILY, with more than 75 works, from 27 September 2023 to 9 August 2024, curated by Julian Cox.[ago-kaws] Its centrepiece, FAMILY of 2021, is a painted bronze of four of his recurring figures posed as a nuclear family.[ago-kaws]

Brooklyn

Paddy Johnson, in The Art Newspaper, gave KAWS credit for skill, especially the move from graffiti to painting and toys. But she found that "nearly every sculpture in the show looks like it's rendered in plastic, even when cast in bronze or aluminium", thought the final rotunda fizzled, and suggested the museum shop was the real show. Her last line: "I felt left out of a party I didn't want to attend."[tan-kaws-2021]

Toronto

The Globe and Mail's critic asked the obvious question of an artist whose cartoon figures are an easy way in: "an entry point to what?" The review found the later work slick and its themes simple, and saw in FAMILY and its companions "an unlikely reach for feeling in the midst of deeply ironic gestures".[globe-kaws]

Our view

Our reading: the two reviews describe the same tension from opposite ends. The figures began as jokes on advertising, such as UNTITLED (HARING) of 1997, painted over a real advertising poster.[ago-kaws] The recent sculptures are sincere: grief, care, family. The surfaces stayed glossy as the subjects grew serious, and that is what both critics found hard to trust.

VerdictWell made and widely loved, and still not persuasive to most critics as more than that. The early altered adverts remain the sharpest work.

articles.title: Eko Nugroho: Lost in Parody, spells that never quite work
articles.dek: Nugroho's 2020 show in Seoul was seen by many only on screen. One critic found the embroideries the strongest part, and the uncertainty in them the point.
articles.body:
Lost in Parody was Eko Nugroho's show at Arario Gallery, Seoul, from 1 September to 24 November 2020. Clara Che Wei Peh reviewed it for Art & Market through the gallery's virtual tour.[artandmarket-eko]

The show

The show mixed acrylic paintings, works on paper and embroidered paintings. Peh notes that embroidery became a major medium for Nugroho from 2007, made with a village workshop in Indonesia.[artandmarket-eko] The largest piece she discusses, A Pot Full of Peace Spells of 2018, is an embroidered painting 275 by 316 cm: four masked figures around a red pot that gives off neon green mist.[artandmarket-eko]

What the critic said

Peh judged the embroideries the strongest works. She read the show as social commentary on love, peace and democracy, delivered in the look of comics and street art. Her favourite piece works by holding back: "Nugroho's painting holds us hostage before we are able to witness the spells' effects."[artandmarket-eko] She was grateful for the virtual format, which let her study dense details closely, while admitting that the feel of the stitching was lost on screen.[artandmarket-eko]

Our view

Our reading: the withheld spell is a good key to Nugroho in general. His masked figures are rarely heroes or villains. They gather, plot and wait. Embroidery suits that mood, because the stitched surface is slow to make and slow to read. A review written from a screen is a limited thing, as Peh says, but she points to what to look for.

VerdictA thoughtful review of a show few saw in person. It makes a good case that the embroideries, not the paintings, carry his ideas best.

articles.title: Faith XLVII: CHANT, a show about paying attention
articles.dek: Delayed a year by lockdown, Faith XLVII's Cape Town show opened in May 2021. One critic read it as an exercise in shared grief, across paint, brass, video and found material.
articles.body:
CHANT was due to open at Everard Read, Cape Town, in April 2020 and was postponed by lockdown.[dm-faith] It finally ran from 5 to 28 May 2021. Misha Krynauw reviewed it for ArtThrob.[artthrob-faith]

The work

Krynauw lists painting, video, photography, sculpture, found materials and drawing. Among the oils is They Say Blood is Heavier Than Water of 2020, 177 by 116 cm, painted after Nicky Newman's photographs of protests in Cape Town against gender-based violence: three arms, two pointing fingers and a raised fist. The Human Cause III, also 2020, is a flag made of brass and wood, 285.5 cm high.[artthrob-faith]

What the critic said

Krynauw read the show as a counter to the numbness of the news cycle, a call to give full attention instead of skimming headlines. The phrase she uses is "mutual mourning": the works hold up moments of pain, from colonialism and inequality to police violence and war, and ask the viewer to share them rather than consume them.[artthrob-faith]

Our view

Our reading: the variety of media is the most telling thing here. Faith XLVII made her name on walls, and a gallery show can feel like a step back from that. CHANT does not try to recreate a mural indoors. It uses slower media, oil on linen and cast brass, for subjects that the street usually only glimpses. Her own words from the time fit the show: "These are not works made to be pretty or decorative."[dm-faith]

VerdictA serious, varied show whose subject is attention itself. Read alongside her murals, it shows a street painter choosing slowness on purpose.

articles.title: Van Gogh: Poets and Lovers, a painter with a plan
articles.dek: The National Gallery's 2024 show gathered 61 works from Arles and Saint-Rémy. Critics gave it top marks, and several argued it finally retired the myth of the mad, tortured artist.
articles.body:
Van Gogh: Poets and Lovers ran at the National Gallery, London, from 14 September 2024 to 19 January 2025.[prospect-vangogh] Martin Bailey counted 47 paintings and 14 drawings, all from the two years Van Gogh spent in the south of France.[tan-vangogh-2024]

What the critics said

Bailey, in The Art Newspaper, gave it five stars: "A magnificent show with important and rarely seen loans." He liked the plain presentation, with numbers on the walls and a free booklet, but noted one cost of the themed rooms: by mixing work from Arles and Saint-Rémy, they make the changes in his style harder to follow.[tan-vangogh-2024]

Diana Carroll, in ArtsHub, called it "a thoughtful and considered exhibition", and pointed to the opening pair of portraits, The Lover and The Poet, as setting up a show about the man as much as the art.[artshub-vangogh]

David McAllister, in Prospect, made the most interesting case. The show reveals no new Van Gogh, he wrote, and that is the point: the tortured-artist story has become a habit that stops us looking. Nothing in the rooms was unknown. What mattered was seeing it plainly, down to five versions of one olive grove in the final room.[prospect-vangogh]

The Sunflowers moment

The show reunited the National Gallery's Sunflowers with the version from the Philadelphia Museum of Art, not lent since Philadelphia bought it in 1963, with La Berceuse between them.[tan-vangogh-2024]

Our view

Our reading: McAllister and Bailey pull in different directions and both are useful. Bailey wants to see development. McAllister wants to see method. Van Gogh's own letters support the second. In July 1890 he wrote of a painting of Daubigny's garden in Auvers as "one of my most carefully thought-out canvases".[letter-651]

VerdictThe best kind of blockbuster: famous pictures, hung simply, with an argument that holds. It made the case for Van Gogh as a planner, not a patient.

articles.title: Kandinsky at the Guggenheims: a collector's eye
articles.dek: Bilbao in 2020 and New York in 2021 both drew on the Guggenheim's founding collection of Kandinsky. The shows were praised for clarity and faulted for saying nothing new.
articles.body:
Two shows of Kandinsky drew on the same source. At Guggenheim Bilbao, Kandinsky ran from 20 November 2020 to 23 May 2021 with 62 paintings and works on paper, all from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York.[si-kandinsky-bilbao] In New York the same collection filled the spiral ramp in Vasily Kandinsky: Around the Circle, on view until September 2022.[nyunews-kandinsky]

What the critics said

David Trigg, in Studio International, found the Bilbao show "superbly presented" and clear about how the paintings change over time. He also said plainly that "it offers no fresh interpretations of his life and work". In his view the real author of the show was Solomon Guggenheim, who bought at every stage of Kandinsky's career: "it is his discerning eye that really shapes this show."[si-kandinsky-bilbao]

In New York, Clara Scholl, writing for NYU's Washington Square News, liked the way the ramp turned the career into a walk. She quoted the museum's own idea, that his was "not a fixed path from representation to abstraction, but rather a circular passage".[nyunews-kandinsky]

Our view

Our reading: Trigg's complaint is fair, and also says something good about the collection. A single collector's purchases, made while the artist was alive, give a rare even view of a whole career. Composition 8, bought in Dessau in 1929, was the first of more than 150 Kandinskys the Guggenheim came to own.[bilbao-comp8] The New York ramp, which forces a slow circling walk, suited a painter who thought of abstraction as a return as much as an arrival.

VerdictClear, handsome collection shows that teach well and argue little. Go for the paintings, and for the history of how they were collected.

articles.title: Rene Matić at the Turner Prize: a flag that says no
articles.dek: In Bradford in 2025 Matić's room was built around a vast white flag. Critics read it as tender, political or, in one case, merely pleasant.
articles.body:
The Turner Prize 2025 exhibition opened at Cartwright Hall, Bradford, in September 2025 and ran until 22 February 2026.[spectator-turner-2025] Rene Matić was shortlisted for the solo show AS OPPOSED TO THE TRUTH at CCA Berlin.[tate-turner-2025] The prize went to Nnena Kalu.[ma-turner-2025]

The room

At its centre hung Untitled (No Place for Violence), 2024, a huge white flag reading "No Place" on one side and "For Violence" on the other. Kadish Morris, in Tate Etc., notes that the words echo statements by Joe Biden and Barack Obama after the attempt on Donald Trump's life in July 2024.[tateetc-turner-2025] Around it leaned the photographs of Feelings Wheel, 2022 to 2025: flags, parties, protests, lovers kissing, shop fronts.[tateetc-turner-2025] On shelves sat Restoration, broken antique Black dolls, which Morris reads as an act of care linked to Matić's father, abandoned as a child in Peterborough.[tateetc-turner-2025]

What the critics said

Millie Lacey, in The State of the Arts, read the flag against sound from pro-Palestinian protests in the room, and concluded: "Matić exposes the contradiction between political rhetoric and violent state action."[sota-turner-2025] Gareth Harris in The Art Newspaper quoted the artist's own aim, to "embarrass the kind of principle of what a flag is supposed to be".[tan-turner-2025]

Digby Warde-Aldam, in The Spectator, was unmoved: "Matic's room is nice enough, in its sub-Wolfgang Tillmans way." He added: "I'm not sure there's much more to it, but it's all beautifully presented."[spectator-turner-2025]

Our view

Our reading: the Tillmans comparison is about the photographs, and it is not unfair, as both artists hang snapshots loosely in groups. But it misses the flag. A flag usually claims a place for a nation. This one claims no place for anything, and the dolls on the other side of the wall turn that refusal into care. The room works because those two ideas sit so close together.

VerdictA quiet room with one loud object, and a fair case that photography, sound and found things can make a political point without shouting.

articles.title: Raven Halfmoon: Flags of Our Mothers, clay that keeps its fingerprints
articles.dek: Halfmoon's touring show of giant stoneware figures opened at the Aldrich in 2023 and moved to Omaha in 2024. Critics wrote about weight, colour and the marks of her hands.
articles.body:
Flags of Our Mothers opened at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in Ridgefield, Connecticut, from 25 June 2023 to 7 January 2024, and moved to the Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts, Omaha, from 18 May to 15 September 2024.[rail-halfmoon][sixty-halfmoon]

What the critics said

The Brooklyn Rail's review was struck first by size. Flagbearer of 2022, built in three stacked parts, stands over twelve feet and weighs 2,400 pounds, and takes up more of the room than anything else.[rail-halfmoon] The review reads the glaze colours as meaningful: red for the soil of Oklahoma and for murdered Indigenous women, black for the clay of the Red River. It quotes Halfmoon in the show's film: "you can see the moment that I laid down the mark."[rail-halfmoon]

River Ian Kerstetter, writing from the Bemis Center for Sixty Inches From Center, gives Flagbearer as 14 feet, so the sources differ on the height. Kerstetter argues that Halfmoon's women are "unambiguously Indigenous both in their features and in their power", and reads her name, written across each piece, as a turn from graffiti's "I was here" to "I am here".[sixty-halfmoon]

Our view

Our reading: both reviews come back to the hand marks, and so should anyone seeing the work. Art schools usually teach potters to smooth a surface. Halfmoon leaves the pushes and scrapes of building coils in place, so a twelve-foot figure still shows the size of the hand that made it. That is what stops the scale from feeling like a monument and keeps it feeling like a person.

VerdictA strong touring show that two very different critics read the same way: as presence, not decoration. The figures are worth seeing in person for the surfaces alone.

articles.title: Ana Segovia: cowboys, cropped
articles.dek: From MOCA in Los Angeles to Frieze London and a 2026 show in New York, Segovia keeps cutting the heroic western figure down to his belt, his hat and his hands.
articles.body:
In two years Ana Segovia has had a first US museum show, MOCA Focus in Los Angeles, a solo booth at Frieze London with kurimanzutto in October 2025, and a first solo show at kurimanzutto New York in autumn 2026.[moca-segovia][nyt-segovia][kurimanzutto-oiaa]

What the critics said

Ray Mark Rinaldi, in The New York Times, called Segovia "a master at directing viewers' gaze". He was writing about Ramón, a series built around an invented cowboy. The paintings crop the body from hip to knee and hide the face, and the titles mislead on purpose: in Ramón Throwing a Rock, he notes, "There is no rock."[nyt-segovia] Rinaldi reads the work as turning macho film heroes upside down, with the jeans and chaps painted in reflective reds that make the eroticism plain.[nyt-segovia]

New York, 2026

The Office of Inter-American Affairs Presents turned to the gaucho of South America. The gallery describes large paintings of single details, a hat, a poncho, a belt, hands holding a mate, "cropped like cinematic close-ups", alongside archive films from the United States agency of 1940 that gives the show its title, and Gambola (Uruguay), a video showing only dancers' legs and feet.[kurimanzutto-oiaa] We have not found an independent review of this show yet, so this is the gallery's account.

Our view

Our reading: the cropping is the critique. Western films sell the hero as a whole body in a wide landscape. Segovia keeps the costume and cuts away the man, so the pose stays and the authority goes. Segovia has said of the Ramón series: "Ramón is my fantasy of who I want to be, or think I am."[another-segovia] That line stops the work from being simple mockery.

VerdictA clear, witty body of work with a single strong device. The open question, which the next shows will answer, is how far one device can go.

articles.title: Dana Awartani: Standing by the ruins, mending as a way of remembering
articles.dek: Awartani's 2025 show at Arnolfini, Bristol, rebuilt a destroyed bathhouse floor in Gaza in unfired brick. One critic found anger and prayer in the same rooms.
articles.body:
Standing by the ruins was Dana Awartani's solo show at Arnolfini, Bristol, from 28 June to 28 September 2025. Oliver Basciano reviewed it for e-flux.[eflux-awartani-ruins]

The work

On the floor were three squares of adobe brick in ochre, white and grey, laid in geometric patterns without cement. Basciano explains that they recreate the washroom tiles of the Hamam al-Sammara, a fourteenth-century bathhouse in Gaza destroyed in 2023.[eflux-awartani-ruins] Overhead hung Come, let me heal your wounds. Let me mend your broken bones, the silk work first shown in Venice in 2024. Small wall pieces of darned silk and typed labels named lost sites, such as the Tetrapylon at Palmyra.[eflux-awartani-ruins]

What the critic said

Basciano framed the show through a saying of the Prophet about mending one's own sandals and clothes, and read the whole show as repair. Knowing what the brick floors copy, he wrote, adds anger to what would otherwise look like calm geometry. He saw a steady pull between politics and something closer to prayer, and called the works "modes of preservation through recreation".[eflux-awartani-ruins] Of a video in which sand is swept away, he wrote: "a physical prayer in which illusion is swept away to reveal what lies beyond".[eflux-awartani-ruins]

Our view

Our reading: the unfired brick is the decision that matters. Adobe is the most ordinary building material there is, and laying it without mortar leaves the floor visibly temporary. A copy that admits it could fall apart is a more honest memorial than a polished replica.

VerdictA careful, moving show in which craft is used as evidence. Basciano's review is the best guide to what each piece copies, and why.

articles.title: Jes Fan: Sites of Wounding, beautiful surfaces that keep a secret
articles.dek: Fan's 2023 Hong Kong show cast knees and torsos in resin and glass, and grew pearls with writing in them. One critic read the beauty as a disguise.
articles.body:
Sites of Wounding: Chapter 1 ran at Empty Gallery, Hong Kong, from 18 March to 24 June 2023. Wong Binghao reviewed it for e-flux.[eflux-fan-wounding]

The work

The sculptures look abstract, but Wong explains that they are cast from knees, chests and torsos. Left and right knee, grafted of 2023 is aqua resin, glass and pigment, with a glass form made by pushing two blowpipes into one goblet so it splits into two chambers.[eflux-fan-wounding] The film Palimpsest, 2023, follows nearly three years of research with scientists at the University of Hong Kong, in which Chinese characters reading "Pearl of the Orient" were implanted in live oysters.[eflux-fan-wounding]

What the critic said

Wong's argument is that the body sources are made deliberately hard to read. Trans artists' work is often received as a display of the body, and Fan refuses that: "the mesmerizing veneers of the exhibited artworks double as disguises". Of the pearls: "Like the pearl it protects, this artwork reveals its meaning only in glimpses."[eflux-fan-wounding]

Our view

Our reading: the oyster is the right image for the whole show. A pearl is what an oyster makes around an injury, and it is beautiful partly because it hides the cause. Fan has said "Art and sciences are essentially just ways of questioning."[mplus-fan] In this show the questions are asked through materials, not explained in labels, and Wong's review is a good way to catch up with them.

VerdictDemanding and quietly beautiful work. Wong shows that the difficulty is chosen, and that it protects as much as it puzzles.

articles.title: Mohamed L'Ghacham: Colorado, a muralist's family album
articles.dek: L'Ghacham's first gallery show gathered nineteen paintings from a single road trip. Writers on his murals and his studio work keep returning to the same word: album.
articles.body:
Mohamed L'Ghacham is best known for walls. Colorado was his first solo show at PDP Gallery, with 19 paintings drawn from a visit to Colorado in May 2018, during a road trip from New York to Los Angeles, and two mural interventions.[jux-lghacham-colorado]

What writers said

Sasha Bogojev, in Juxtapoz, describes camping trips, interiors and household scenes, and says that "each work invites a browse through a family photo album". He notes that the figures are almost faceless, and that "their surroundings and actions dictate the mood and narrative".[jux-lghacham-colorado] This is closer to a gallery report than a critical review. We have not found an independent review of the show.

Writing about the murals in Colossal, Andrew LaSane made a similar point. L'Ghacham paints from old family photographs, often choosing the accidental shots, and uses loose, layered strokes that ask the viewer to step back before a face comes together.[colossal-lghacham-2019]

Our view

Our reading: the faceless figures are what carry over from wall to canvas. On a wall, a face blurred from across the street lets passers-by see their own relatives. On a canvas, seen close, the same blur reads as memory fading. The studio paintings are smaller and quieter, but they show the method more clearly than the murals can.

VerdictA modest first show that is most useful as a key to the murals. The album idea is not ours, but it fits.

articles.title: Andy Warhol at Tate Modern: the man behind the brand
articles.dek: Tate's 2020 retrospective opened days before lockdown. Critics agreed it was handsome and personal, and argued about the late work and the queer reading.
articles.body:
Andy Warhol opened at Tate Modern on 12 March 2020, closed almost at once because of the pandemic, and was due to run until 6 September 2020. It was curated by Gregor Muir and Fiontán Moran with Yilmaz Dziewior and Stephan Diederich of Museum Ludwig, Cologne.[tan-warhol-2020]

What the critics said

Brian Allen, in The Art Newspaper, thought Warhol's own presence was the show's strength and the installation well done, but found the 1970s and 1980s work weaker. He was not persuaded by the curators' claim that Warhol put queer identity at the centre of Pop. Still, "it's a fine exhibition and introduces Warhol to a new generation."[tan-warhol-2020]

The Frieze review took the opposite view of the late work. It rejected the usual story of decline after Warhol was shot, and saw "all-of-a-piece Warhol, working full throttle for four solid decades". It found Sixty Last Suppers of 1986 had "lost its religiosity".[frieze-warhol-2020]

Beth Williamson, in Studio International, read the show as a story of loss, and the same late painting as a memorial, linked to the Aids-related death of Warhol's partner. She found Silver Clouds and the restaged light show Exploding Plastic Inevitable joyful.[si-warhol-2020]

Our view

Our reading: the disagreement over the late work is the most useful thing in these reviews. The silkscreen, which Warhol took up in 1962 to repeat images quickly, looks the same in 1962 and 1986.[si-warhol-2020] What changes is what he chose to repeat: film stars, then skulls, then the Last Supper. Whether that is decline or continuity depends on whether you look at the method or the subject.

VerdictA personal, well hung retrospective, unlucky in its timing. The reviews together make the best case yet for taking the late work seriously.

articles.title: ANTI-FRIEZE: what melts when the art market is put on ice
